items.body: Across its seventeen tracks, Wahj brings together electronics, industrial textures, processed strings, Arabic vocal traditions and fractured rhythms in combinations that keep changing shape. Individual elements remain recognisable without settling into familiar forms, while images of voice, disappearance, radiance and return recur throughout the album. Wahj took shape over five years, and the events of that period inevitably entered the music. As Toni Geitani explains in the accompanying interview, the album was not initially conceived as a meditation on collapse. The idea emerged gradually as the circumstances surrounding its composition changed. Collapse here is not a single catastrophic moment. Ruin exists alongside what persists, with Geitani attentive to the lives and voices that political violence can obscure. This runs through the lyrics as well as the music. Voices appear and disappear, sometimes sounding like invocations, sometimes carrying fragments of collective memory. On the brief “Sawtuka”, Geitani repeats, “Raise your voice higher and higher. Even if they bind you, even if they take you through death, the echo of your voice will remain forever.” The refrain turns persistence itself into an act of resistance. “2092” projects the idea into an imagined future in which “every fascist has fallen, and their glory belongs to nothingness,” before asking, “Does love remain when everything has vanished?” “Hal”, “Ruwaydan Ruwaydan” and the extended instrumental closer “Madda Mudadda” draw on ritual, repetition and moments of ecstatic release, with their meanings left open. The title, Wahj, points towards radiance, although Geitani gives the word no easy redemptive meaning. Light appears amid destruction, sometimes faintly, and does not cancel what surrounds it. In “Tuyoor”, the image is carried by birds: “The birds flying above you do not belong to the ruler who oppressed you. They watch the sky, not the earth beneath you.” The image opens a space outside the authority of the ruler, even while that authority continues to shape life below. Throughout Wahj, Geitani keeps returning to such spaces: voices that outlast attempts to silence them, traces of love after disappearance, and forms of life that continue amid devastation. To discuss the making of Wahj, we approched Toni Geitani directly. Wahj is described as an album about collapse, but one that refuses to remain trapped within its concept. Across the record, images of ruin, mourning, exile, and disappearance are constantly accompanied by gestures toward radiance, return, and endurance. How did you approach balancing these opposing forces while writing the album? I didn’t start working on the album with any intention of a “theme”, in this case collapse. I also wasn’t trying to narrow down the album to one thematic focus. It was an intuitive process that mostly guided the work. But it is true that as the project developed over five years, a lot of horrific events unfolded; consecutively and sometimes simultaneously. This naturally affected the relation to my work in a way that pushed me into ending up with these tracks, which I could eventually describe as being about collapse. By saying that the album refuses to be reduced to collapse, I’m intentionally pushing back against the idea that collapse is only a sudden, singular catastrophe. I was born in the 1990s in post-civil-war Lebanon, so from early on I was surrounded by war stories told by family and friends. After continuous exposure to these stories throughout my life, I came to understand that they were not stories of the past only, but of a collapse that kept resurfacing in different forms. At the same time, however, I was also exposed to another image of collapse that dominated global media and felt especially present in my teens in the 2000s. It was that of an image imported from the West, romanticized, and flattened into spectacle. It also ignores how, for some populations, collapse is already ongoing rather than a problem of the future or an isolated incident that can be inherited and prolonged. That difference matters to me because, for many of us, imperialism, colonialism, and capitalism are not warnings of an apocalypse to come, but they morph to become ongoing and almost fixed conditions. So when I was writing Wahj, I didn’t feel that I was trying to balance opposing forces simply because I do not see them as opposing, but inevitably coexisting. Instead, I was trying to remain faithful to everything catastrophe-centered narratives tend to erase: memory, resistance, regeneration, and the human capacity to continue. They are what must be reclaimed from within it. The lyrics repeatedly return to voices, echoes, and acts of calling out across distance. In “Sawtuka” (“Your Voice”), for example, the refrain insists that a voice survives even imprisonment or death, while tracks like “2092” and “Tuyoor” are structured around questions of who is listening and who remains absent. What role does the voice play in Wahj—as memory, resistance, testimony, or something else entirely? For this album, I composed the music before writing the lyrics. I would often record a vocal melody, sometimes with words that made sense and sometimes not, simply to find a fitting flow and have it as a placeholder until the final vocal recording. But before I began writing and recording the lyrics, the genocide in Gaza began alongside the war on Lebanon in 2023, so I stopped working on the album because I felt uneasy about prioritizing it. At that point, nothing made sense anymore. But somehow, by the beginning of 2025, I found the motivation to finish the project, and thus the lyrics were written. In my opinion, the voice can hold many roles at once, including the ones mentioned in the question. It is not intended to be a tool for meaning-making, but rather a presence moving through space, carrying the emotional and political conditions of that space with it. However, its position is immanent rather than observational. It does not stand outside the world to explain it. Instead, it emerges from within that world and continually reaches outward, while refusing to die. The lyrics inevitably reflect the experience of witnessing a 24/7 livestreamed ongoing Palestinian genocide, and the rage, injustice, betrayal, pain, and constant aggression we have been dealing with for many years. However, I do not wish to limit the album’s interpretation to the events of the past three years. As I mentioned earlier, collapse is not a one-time event or a singular fall, but I insist that it emerges from an ongoing oppression imposed on us by the same death machine. Musically, the album moves between processed classical instruments, layālī-inspired vocal passages, industrial textures, dark ambient atmospheres, and fractured electronic rhythms without ever fully settling into any one genre. Did you begin with a clear sonic vision for Wahj, or did this hybrid language emerge gradually during the five years of recording between 2021 and 2025? I did begin with a fairly clear sonic vision for Wahj, in the sense that from the beginning I wanted it to explore different genres and subgenres while still remaining rooted in electronics. What emerged gradually was not that intention itself, but the specific language the album took on through time, collaboration, experimentation, and everything that happened across those years. After releasing my first album in 2018, I wanted to keep exploring and collaborating before putting out another record. Between 2018 and 2020, I performed many live shows in Lebanon, where improvisation became an important space for testing new ideas and compositions. Over time, this left me with more than a hundred sketches, from which I selected the ones that felt less attached to a single genre and more committed to a shared atmosphere and universe, even if that universe itself remains unstable and fluctuating. When I began my studies at the Conservatorium van Amsterdam in 2021, that process expanded further. Being surrounded by many different kinds of musicians pushed me to explore classical instrumentation, processing, and different digital approaches in ways I had not tried beforehand. I recorded many phrases and ideas with musicians there, often without knowing exactly what their final form would be, because part of the process was discovering how their playing could be transformed and absorbed into the album’s sonic world. In that sense, the hybrid language of the record was both intended and gradually revealed. As mentioned earlier, I returned to working on the album in the beginning of 2025, and that final period inevitably shaped the work in a profound way. So while the album’s sonic foundation was there from the beginning, its final form was shaped by a long process of experimentation, disruption, and response to the world it was being made within. Several tracks evoke futures rather than simply documenting the present. The title “2092,” in particular, imagines a distant horizon where “every fascist has fallen and their glory belongs to nothingness,” while love and memory continue to endure. What attracted you to speculative or future-oriented thinking as a way of responding to contemporary political realities? I would like to make a distinction between futurism as typically understood through a Eurocentric lens which is rooted in Euro-American frameworks and historically entangled with imperialism and fascism – and counterfuturism that emerged from the Global South which functions to complicate normalized notions of time and technology rather than projecting a single vision of the future. And this is precisely what I intend to convey in the practice of imagining futures in the album, which attempt to articulate a cultural politics of time and become a means of writing alternative histories that distance themselves from any established history already written. This could mean reclaiming the right to think beyond imperialist scripts through collective knowledge, agency, and world-making rather than celebrating rupture, domination, or heroic modernity. In other words, I’m trying to open possibilities from within collapse, and thus, this framework differs from futurism as an approach for technocratic future-thinking. For example in “2092”, I try to treat the future as a tool to ask whose futures have been denied or flattened, instead of assuming it operates in a single path of progress. The political visions I sing about are not predictions, but they gesture toward an intense need to imagine the aftermath of collapse in the hope that something promising might emerge from it. That being said, I don’t intend for my songs to be frontal or overly obvious in their interpretation, and I welcome listeners to bring different meanings to them. You wrote a master’s thesis titled Sampling as a Political Medium, examining questions of power, appropriation, and cultural memory. Wahj incorporates repurposed regional sounds and references while constructing an entirely new sonic language. How has your thinking about sampling evolved since that research, and how do those ideas inform the album’s relationship to Arabic musical traditions and collective memory? My thinking on sampling has certainly evolved, although I do not see it as a linear progression that concluded with my thesis. The research was conducted alongside the creation of the album and I continue to work with samples, therefore I am always interacting with this topic. Throughout Wahj, I work with both political and non-political samples that either have a political or non-political intention. For example, samples from my personal life, my urban surroundings, and of traditional instruments, the choice is more nuanced because it’s integrated and processed within the soundscape and ambient textures. However, for samples that are more frontal and forward, like the sampling of Amal Dunqul’s poem, “Spartacus’ Last Words” in “Madda Mudadda” the intention is more clearly deliberate and explicit. These choices are bound to spill into collective memory, as I am borrowing sounds from my surroundings and heritage. Take the sample of Lebanese singers Sabah, Wadih El Safi, and Walid Gholmieh in “Wasla”; I was drawn to their voices for reasons I can’t quite articulate. But the moment I tried fitting the sample into the track, it felt seamless. My sampling choices are meant to re-activate archive sound, and insert these historical moments into the present to let them speak again through a different context. All voice samples from the album come from televised interviews, and I chose them not only for their raw, untampered sound, but also because they carry something of the world they were recorded in. To sample them is to pull them back into light and reactivate voices forced to be erased for new audiences, while also making visible the power structures that determine whose memory is preserved and who is erased from the record. Ultimately, these sampling choices are always, in some way, in conversation with the cultural memory I carry, bringing the historical in contact with the contemporary. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Some promotion arrives generously late, but with this debut album by the Australian solo project Empty Vessel, I felt it was more than necessary to give it some attention anyway. Tom Wojcicki is an artist unknown to most, who released the album “Ruin Value” in the spring of 2025, an opus consisting of eight tracks. What I hear here defies all imagination: an absolute masterpiece in which the artist blends Industrial, Cinematic, and Ritual elements in a remarkably refined manner. He creates a tormented atmosphere of overwhelming sounds, with percussion effects that reverberate like drones. That overwhelming quality, in particular, is almost indescribable. Rarely have I encountered an artist capable of creating sounds as intense, present, and tormented as those of Empty Vessel. The tracks can be repetitive at times, but because of their sheer intensity, you are truly blown away. Before you know it, you are trapped in a sonic web of terrifying and illusory images. The album is a succession of insane tracks, meaning that you discover one highlight after another. If you are a fan of the genres mentioned above and are not yet familiar with Empty Vessel, I would simply recommend buying this album without listening to it beforehand. An absolute masterpiece, and it will not be easy to follow this up with an equally powerful successor. (Rating:9). Listen to “Scattered Pieces Of Her”: Scattered Pieces Of Her by Empty Vessel About Empty Vessel Empty Vessel is the solo industrial and power electronics project of Australian artist Tom Wojcicki. “Ruin Value” was released on 14 April 2025 through the German label Dunkelheit Produktionen as a hand-numbered CD limited to 200 copies with a 4-page booklet, plus a digital edition, under catalog number DP179CD. The album runs eight tracks, opening with “Scattered Pieces Of Her” and closing with “Zero Fetish”. Empty Vessel has also recorded under the names Droid Sector, Broken Fingers, Glass Barbeque, Aurora Seven and Cockroach Diocese. “Ruin Value” is Empty Vessel’s first release to be reviewed on Side-Line.

items.body: Pendulum is a singular piano trio featuring French pianist Benoît Delbecq with Danish double bass player Jonas Westergaard and drummer Peter Bruun (both Westergaard and Bruun have collaborated before with fellow Danish pianist Søren Kjærgaard). Bruun initiated this trio in 2024 as part of his ambitious research project exploring new approaches to musical time (Multitemporal movement and embodiment through Rhythmic Design at The Danish National Academy of Music). The Pendulum trio investigates all aspects of this classic format, including the most basic sensibilities of space and time, avoiding rigid structures, allowing instead for balance, elegance and fluidity. It challenges us to listen to its music as resonant arcs or shared fields of presence rather than defined by linear time, and explores new ways to transform free improvisation gravity into groove. Delbeq suggested that the trio will play with the presence of physical pendulums on stage, symbolizing the elasticity of time and giving a sense of pulse. These oscillating bodies guide the subtle, cyclical shifts in the music, which, paradoxically, feels familiar: music that sways and breathes, while finding rhythm in the inevitability of motion. The trio releases its eight-volume EP series, Arcs , nearly three hours of music, in a monthly release cycle that began in May and will conclude in December 2026. These Arcs offer Pendulum’s idiosyncratic, enigmatic, lyrical universe, in which metric relations, shifting balances, and elastic phrasing are woven together in a kaleidoscopic manner. Each volume swings on its own terms, with no intention to offer a linear narrative, and uses distinct compositional fragments, notated and graphic scores. But the whole project accumulates into an open body of work that allows us to feel how time bends, breathes, and searches for an elusive balance. The Pendulum trio invites listeners to form their own path through the eight volumes and discover different insights and relations in their own time. Arc No. 1 Pendulum describes this volume: “Time leans before it moves. Motion unfolds patiently, stretching and rebounding with quiet elasticity. What propels the arc is not force but attentiveness, which allows duration to bend and return without breaking. Each swing carries clarity and restraint, revealing time as something more shaped than measured”. The trio suggests sparse, deep listening, labyrinthine architectures with patient and subtle, cyclical-rhythmic shifts, best captured in the aptly titled, 17-minute minimalist “Exercice Elastique”, that patiently gravitates into a most delicate, vulnerable, quite irreverent groove. Arc No. 2 “Afterwards appears before it is recognized. Movement writes itself into space, leaving subtle traces that guide listening rather than direction. Rhythms form paths, both adaptable and responsive, where perception stretches between memory and anticipation. The arc remains fluid, shaped by change rather than arrival”. Pendulum sketches an almost abstract, empty map, from which it begins to imagine possible contours and paths, and how to find its inner, spatial logic, and its subtle rhythmic shifts, finally realized on “Plasticity”. Arc No. 3 “Movement turns inward. Each gesture is weighted, deliberate, and reduced to necessity. Time thickens as motion slows, inviting attention to settle inside the smallest shifts. The arc transforms discreetly, as intensity is held beneath restraint. Balance is discovered through presence, not display”. The 31-minute “Buto” corresponds with the hyper-slow and hyper-controlled motion of the Japanese avant-dance theatre, Butō (舞踏), that resists and fixated conception of time. Pendulum’s fragile balance was realized through an austere, cryptic, and often almost silent presence that keeps triggering our imagination, and not by technical display or mastery. Arc No. 4 “Wooden time moves with grain and resistance. Motion creaks, sways, and negotiates its own structure. Oscillation becomes tactile, shaped by friction and patience. The arc holds multiple possibilities at once, allowing form and freedom to coexist without resolution. The rings of time are both counted and counting”. The trio focuses on its essence, the ever-negotiated arcs that blur the distinction between form and freedom, and question our conception of linear time, turning it into a spiritual riddle, a kōan. Arc No. 5 “A phase shifts nearly unnoticed. Motion lightens, stepping carefully through softened contours. Layers thin and overlap, revealing phrasing where gestures begin and fade. The arc listens closely to its own balance, finding meaning in nuance rather than emphasis. The push and pull are their own reason for being”. Pendulum refines its fragile, nuanced equilibrium with melodic threads that patiently, hesitantly flirt with familiar, playful, and resonant piano trio dynamics. Arc No. 6 (to be released on October 10) “Momenta accumulate through return. Motion becomes practiced, framed by shared gravity and memory. Energy circulates without urgency, shaped by repetition and transformation. The past is present and future at once”. A further, urgent, cyclical rhythmic refinement is offered, faithfully captured in the short pieces “Arc” and “Dance”, shaped by nuanced repetitions and transformations. Arc No. 7 (to be released on November 9) “Time folds into itself. Multiple cycles coexist, asymmetrical yet connected. Movement breathes across layered durations, allowing contradiction to remain unresolved. The arc sustains density without weight, continuity without uniformity. Listening is wide enough to hold all the all of it”. Pendulum’s music plays a touch-and-go game in its own fragmented musical continuum, sustaining density without weight, continuity without uniformity, but with more structural focus. Arc No. 8 (to be released on December 9) “Strange tools reveal their logic through use. Motion disperses, leaving resonance rather than momentum. What remains feels everywhere at once, absorbed into space and attention. The arc settles without closing, as stillness carries the last trace of movement forward. It is the beginning of the end and the end of the beginning”. The concluding volume is not an end to this fascinating journey but a sort of beginning. The Pendulum trio already inhabited its own elastic conception of time, as the devoted listeners to this journey, and has established its idiosyncratic language. But Pendulum’s music tells us something deeper about life and the inevitable changes we experience throughout life. This trio asks us to adapt our time sensibility to its subtle transformations, fully embrace and be deeply attuned to our own ubiquitous cyclical and oscillating arcs, as we move forward, attempting to maintain an elusive balance. <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-1">Opening Arcs: Arc No. 1 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-2">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 2 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-3">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 3 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-4">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 4 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-5">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 5 by ILK</a > Email This BlogThis! items._cn_summary: Pendulum 是一支由法国钢琴家 Benoît Delbecq 与丹麦低音提琴手 Jonas Westergaard、鼓手 Peter Bruun 组成的钢琴三重奏。该项目源自 Bruun 在丹麦皇家音乐学院发起的多元时间节奏研究计划，探索音乐中时间与空间的弹性感知。三重奏摒弃线性时间结构，以钟摆的往复运动为隐喻，构建回旋式、碎片化的音响弧线。八卷 EP 系列每月释出一卷，总时长近三小时，融合记谱法与图形谱作曲素材，在即兴自由与律动引力之间寻找平衡。乐评特别提及 17 分钟的极简主义作品《Exercice Elastique》，呈现细腻脆弱而近乎不敬的节奏重力。整张专辑将计量关系、动态平衡与弹性乐句编织成万花筒般的听觉宇宙，邀请听众按自己的节奏穿越。

items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comAn outstanding album. The Chilean ensemble Asceta has established itself as one of those collectives you simply have to know if you are a fan of music made with extraordinary care and musicianship. Guided by the creative spirit of Rodrigo Maccioni, the band delivers an album in 2026 that, although there are still several months left in the year, could very well be considered the best Rock in Opposition and avant-prog release of the year. "The Fool Leading The Blind" is the title of the Chileans' third full-length release, an ambitious album that, across fifty three minutes, offers five compositions in which magic, social criticism, and music of the highest caliber take center stage. Everything begins with the album's title track, a twenty one minute suite that can be ominous at times, frenetic at others, and remarkably calm in between. The first three minutes are somewhat contemplative, as something gradually begins to take shape. Strings and drums establish a semi-slow rhythm that slowly builds until, around the four minute mark, the first explosion of rock arrives. Rock in Opposition, indeed, because the criticism directed toward our world and our politics is implicit throughout the piece, and the musicians express it through their constantly shifting yet remarkably intelligent way of communicating. I love the unexpected rhythmic changes, the moments when the energy and pulse suddenly rise, and the way every instrument introduces its own notes and ideas before converging into an incredibly solid composition that eventually leads us toward ecstasy. There is something beautiful about the way these musicians organize themselves to construct their music. I only wish that, as a society, we could demonstrate this same kind of organization when it comes to confronting bad governments and defending our land. After this emotional roller coaster, Asceta offers us the somber "Temple of Mirrors". Its opening minute is somewhat dissonant, with scattered sounds appearing here and there without any clearly defined form. Then, little by little, a structure begins to emerge, bringing clearer sounds and direction. Progressive music, naturally, but also classical music, an endless palette of colors and textures, and a remarkable convergence between acoustic and electric elements, as beautifully demonstrated by the guitar. Strings introduce the creepy and ominous atmosphere of "When They Arrive". Gradually, instruments such as bassoon, drums, and clarinet join the landscape, creating a dark environment in which a sense of unease comes naturally. There are brief bursts of intensity that could easily startle an unsuspecting listener, but there are also moments of harmony in which we can look around and decide which path to take. This is highly visual music, and every listen can inspire completely different stories in the listener's mind. There are passages that evoke After Crying or Art Zoyd. Wonderful. With "Everything Stopped", a frenetic and semi-chaotic rhythm takes over, constantly contrasted by pauses filled with cadence but also nervous energy. The ensemble creates fascinating musical connections. At times the strings take the spotlight, at others the winds or the drums, yet there is always a beautiful cohesion that serves as the thread connecting their performances. The music here is never linear, and that may initially turn away listeners who are not comfortable with such an approach. But once you connect with it, a genuine synergy develops, and it remains intact until the very end of the album. Speaking of endings, this magnificent record concludes with "Memento Mori", a ten minute composition that is colorful and multifaceted, filled with playful changes that bring brightness while contrasting beautifully with darker passages. The bass establishes an ongoing conversation with the clarinet and oboe, and as usual, the Chileans deliver a dose of avant-garde music of the highest caliber, something no fan of this particular musical territory should overlook. A well deserved round of applause for Asceta, lovers of art and natural opposers by conviction. May their talent and passion continue to drive them toward creating music as rewarding as this.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 988Tangerine Dream is a progressive electronic rock band that was founded in Berlin, Germany in 1967 by Edgar Froese, Klaus Schulze and Conrad Schnitzler. The band was among the earlier explorers of a new musical universe opened by electronic instruments. Tangerine Dream's music was born as a psychedelic journey in the heavens, and, aided by the new electronic keyboards, the band transformed into a contemplative survey of the universe. By borrowing from the impressionistic painting, (notably of Salvador Dali), the ecclesiastic music, the minimalist avant-garde, and the Eastern transcendental philosophy, Tangerine Dream invented "kosmische music", one of the most influential musical genres.Tangerine Dream released their debut studio work "Electronic Meditation" in 1970 with Froese, Schulze and Schnitzler. Still, "Electronic Meditation" isn't properly an electronic album. It consists mainly of experimental noises performed with classic rock instruments. So, it's more a rock album made with rock instruments. Actually it's a krautrock album, the musical style invented by the German musicians in the late of the 60's and early of the 70's. It was only on their second album "Alpha Centauri" that the synthesizers came into play. After the release of "Electronic Meditation", each member went his own separate way. The only member that remained in Tangerine Dream was Froese. With Froese, Christopher Franke and Steve Schroyder on the line up, the band released their second work "Alpha Centauri"."Alpha Centauri" is the second album of Tangerine Dream, released in 1971. The line up is Edgar Froese (voice, guitar, bass, organ, Fx and Mellotron), Steve Schroyder (voice, Hammond & Farfisa organs, electronics and percussion) and Christopher Franke (flute, piano, harp, zither, VCS 3 synthesizer, drums and percussion). "Alpha Centauri" also had the participation of Udo Dennenberg (voice and flute), Roland Paulick (VCS 3 synthesizer) and Peter Baumann (organ).As I mentioned above, "Alpha Centauri" is the first really electronic progressive rock album released by the band and where we can see for the first time the use of synthesizers by Tangerine Dream. The line up on the album consisted of a guitarist, a percussionist, a flutist and three keyboardists recording the three improvised jams of "Alpha Centauri" that defined the genre. Here, we can also see the presence, for the first time, of what is considered the best line up of the band, Froese, Franke and Baumann, despite the latter only appearing as guest. As happened with their debut work, "Alpha Centauri" became the only album with this official line up, Froese, Franke and Schroyder. And it became also tremendously closer to what Tangerine Dream would be all about than what their debut had been. Sure, it still sounded rather primitive and low-budget, but Tangerine Dream had now clearly discovered that spacey, atmospheric and dreamy experimental electronic music was the way to go for them. It would be completely proven with their next album "Zeit"."Alpha Centauri" has three tracks. "Sunrise In The Third System" contains some slow spacey sounds and effects. It's a stealthy and hypnotic piece, with a dense organ and a ghostly flute. It has a clear nod to Pink Floyd thanks to the sound of the organ. It forms a perfect introduction to the main cosmic journey, a kind of decompression chamber that helps the listener get acclimated to the alien landscape of Tangerine Dream's musical world. "Fly And Collision Of Comas Sola" slowly builds a heroic theme that eventually crashes into chaos. The track starts with a synthesizer and an organ in the background. The organ makes its appearance to establish the mattress on which flutes and synths build enveloping and disturbing sounds. As the song progresses, the drums appear closing with an abrupt ending. It allows us to envision great things in the future band's history. The title track is the centre piece of the album. It's an interesting improvisation based around spacey electronic sounds, organs and Froese's guitar. At the end goes into a poem spoken in German and climaxes into one of the few cases of human vocal-harmonies on a band's album. The flute makes a fine atmospheric contrast. It's an incredible spacey and timeless experience. You got the impression of leaving this world. It paves way for everything on their next album "Zeit" to all their famous lengthy epics like the title track on "Phaedra".Conclusion: As I mentioned above, "Alpha Centauri" is considered as the first electronic space album. It marks the transition from the krautrock to the electronic bubbling sound of their albums "Zeit" and "Atem" in their Pink phase. If "Electronic Meditation" had seemed better suited to a horror film, "Alpha Centauri" is firmly in the science fiction camp. The structure of the album would prove to be very representative for the several albums to come from the band, with one side long title track and a couple of "shorter" tracks on the other side. So, despite some technical shortcomings, "Alpha Centauri" was an important release in the musical evolution of Tangerine Dream. The mysterious cover painting and art design, by Edgar Froese and his wife at the time, Monique Froese, contribute directly to the album's character. As products of the psych era, "Alpha Centauri", "Zeit" and "Atem", are fine nuggets, even if the best was yet to come.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — There are many factors at play with this soundtrack. First of all, it is worth noting that soundtracks often inspire great electronic music albums, given the genre's inherently cinematic and atmospheric nature, as seen with Klaus Schulze's Body Love. Edgar Froese, his bandmate in Tangerine Dream, turned the score for Wolf Gremm's film into his own sixth solo album. The movie also marked the final screen appearance of the German director Rainer Werner Fassbinder as an actor. Based on the novel Murder on the 31st Floor by Per Wahl��, the story is set in a future Germany where a private corporation holds power and all societal problems appear to have been solved, until a group calling itself "Kamikaze" issues a bomb threat. Detective Jansen (Fassbinder), clad in his signature leopard-print suit, then uncovers unexpected and deeply sinister connections and mysteries. The track "Videophonic" immediately immerses the listener in a sci-fi atmosphere; the music transcends standard synthesizer-based electronics, evoking the mysterious, perilous vibe of Krautrock."Vitamin C" is almost danceable, yet driven by a magnetic, funky groove; beneath the main rhythm lies a synthesizer wash that adds a progressive sheen, allowing the track to build, shift, evolve, and unfold organically. "Krismopompas" reminded me of Air, even though this album predates them, featuring dissonant notes; while knowing the film's plot helps, the track stands perfectly well on its own thanks to its strong melodic content. "Police Disco" shows traces of Vangelis but possesses an restless quality that lends it extreme dynamism; subtle classical influences lurk in the background, and there are echoes of Pink Floyd, specifically the Echoes era, giving the album an experimental edge that makes it compelling.With its electronic percussion, Police Therapy Center feels more rooted in the 80s; yet, there are underlying keyboard layers, like out-of-tune violins, providing subtle accompaniment, while the style shifts instantly to a highly martial funeral march on "Blue Panther." "Unexpected Death" is almost psychedelic, a realm where electronics also lend themselves well, acting as a malleable, mutating substance.Flying Kamikaze is ambient music with a spacey, ethereal vibe, reminiscent of Popol Vuh's work on Fitzcarraldo. Yet it is dark and mysterious, reflecting both the natural world and the ominous Berlin of this dark utopia. "Tower Block" conveys that feverish, concrete-laden urban atmosphere translated into music, while the closing track "The 31st Floor", which alludes to the original novel, broadens the horizon; blending electronica with the futuristic Krautrock style of Can's "Spoon" (from Ege Bamyasi) and straddling the line between film noir and dystopian sci-fi, Kamikaze 1989 showcased many of Froese's great strengths as a composer dedicated to illustrating mental imagery while maintaining his artistic independence.
items._cn_summary: 这是Edgar Froese为Wolf Gremm导演的科幻电影Kamikaze 1989创作的原声专辑，同时作为他的第六张个人专辑发行。整张作品以合成器为主导，营造出浓重的未来主义与赛博朋克氛围，与影片所描绘的反乌托邦德国背景高度契合。音乐在电子节拍与氛围音景之间自由切换，融合了Krautrock的不协和张力、funky律动以及暗色调的电影叙事感。多首曲目展现出不同的情绪侧面：从Videophonic的神秘危险感，到Vitamin C的舞曲化律动，再到Blue Panther的军事葬礼进行曲，以及结尾的环境空间感。评论指出其与Vangelis、Pink Floyd、Popol Vuh、Can等艺术家的风格关联，同时强调Froese在保持艺术独立性的同时，成功将视觉意象转化为听觉体验，是一部兼具叙事性与独立艺术价值的电子作品。

It took me 20 listens before I started even tolerating it. However, after 30 listens, I can say it's a masterpiece of avant-prog. The Captain's voice has really grown on me, and so has the wonderful musicianship. My favorite track and the most essential track off of this album is sweet sweet bulbs. I really have no idea how to say more about this album because it is simply indescribable. I'm looking forward to exploring some more of Beefheart's works. And everyone around me now has to deal with me doing my impression of the hilarious vocals on this album.
items._cn_summary: 这张1969年的专辑被定位为前卫摇滚领域的经典之作，以其极度怪异的结构和不协和的声音著称。评论者经历反复聆听才逐渐接受其独特魅力，形容其难以用语言描述。专辑中Captain Beefheart的嗓音表现极具辨识度，从嘶吼到怪诞唱腔变化莫测，乐手们展现出精湛而自由的器乐演奏能力。推荐曲目Sweet Sweet Bulbs被认为是整张专辑最具代表性的核心作品。整体制作打破常规摇滚框架，融合了自由爵士、布鲁斯和实验音乐元素，形成一种近乎原始的混乱美学。这张作品对开放性聆听有较高要求，适合愿意投入时间探索非常规声音的听众。

items.body: The Sound Veil Society‘s debut album “Things We Kept” is built around an unusual kind of intensity. The record rarely reaches for aggression or dramatic excess; instead, emotional weight accumulates through restraint, space, repetition and the careful relationship between voice, electronics and silence. That became even clearer to me after seeing the duo at E-Only before spending more time with the album. Live, the songs seemed capable of becoming physically larger without sacrificing the intimacy they carry on record. The Swedish-Norwegian project brings together Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson, two musicians with extensive histories in Nordic electronic music, but “Things We Kept” does not sound like an exercise in accumulated experience or genre expertise. The more interesting question is what happens when experience becomes instinct: when musicians know enough to stop demonstrating what they know and instead concentrate on what a song actually needs. Released on 11 September 2026 through Progress Productions, “Things We Kept” is the duo’s first full-length album. Its title becomes more revealing as the record unfolds. What we keep is not necessarily what we consciously choose to preserve. Memory, grief, unfinished conversations, attachments and previous versions of ourselves remain present long after circumstances have changed. That tension between movement and emotional permanence runs quietly through an album whose apparent delicacy repeatedly turns out to carry considerable force. The Sound Veil Society interview Karo: I saw you at E-Only before hearing “Things We Kept”, and what struck me was that the performance generated enormous emotional pressure without relying on aggression or theatrical excess. Is restraint something you consciously build into The Sound Veil Society, or is it simply where the two of you naturally meet? The Sound Veil Society: It’s the natural way for us to express ourselves, and TSVS is the outlet where we can give these feelings and emotions free space in our performance, both on record and live. Karo: “Things We Kept” is a debut album made by musicians who are anything but beginners. Does starting a new project after years of experience give you greater freedom, or does experience make it harder to surprise yourselves because you already know too well what works? The Sound Veil Society: Good question! In a way, it gives us more freedom, as we use our experience together with what we have learned over the years to create something new. But it might just be the circle of life, as we evolve through different phases in our lives, with new experiences and so on. And it would be boring to repeat ourselves, so to trigger creativity and motivation, we just do what we like and hopefully someone else likes it as well. Karo: The album feels remarkably coherent across music, lyrics, photography, videos and the physical booklet. Did you think of “Things We Kept” as a complete world from the beginning, or did that visual and emotional language gradually reveal itself while the music was taking shape? The Sound Veil Society: We did have an idea from the beginning to be very visual in what we do as TSVS. The album itself is a result of our journey in making it. After a year or so of making a lot of demos, we decided where we wanted to take our sound, and after that everything just fell into place. “Things We Kept” became a complete world through the process and, indeed, there is a thought behind the booklet, videos and music completing each other. Karo: There is something almost paradoxical about this record: it sounds delicate, but never weak. I kept thinking of tempered glass: transparent, apparently fragile, yet internally capable of carrying enormous force. Where does that balance between vulnerability and strength come from in your writing? The Sound Veil Society: Really like your reflection of the record! It reflects quite well who we are as people, in a way, as both of us are emotional beings, with our share of struggles both in the past and present. But that can also be used as a strength, because you need a certain amount of strength to deal with the challenges in life. So for us it is a very natural process and nothing we “try” to do. It just happens that way. Karo: The lyrics repeatedly return to movement: leaving, running, waiting, returning, searching for air. Yet emotionally, many of the characters seem unable to escape what they carry with them. Were you consciously interested in the difference between physically moving on and actually changing? The Sound Veil Society: Not really. It is just our way of describing thoughts and feelings that are close to us, or stories and reflections that have inspired us over the years. Karo: The title “Things We Kept” becomes more interesting the longer one spends with the record, because what people keep is often not something they would consciously choose: grief, unfinished conversations, versions of other people, even destructive attachments. What does “keeping” mean to you in the context of this album? The Sound Veil Society: We think that everything we experience, be it good or bad, stays with us to some degree, even when we have almost forgotten about it, because it shapes us into who we are right now. Without all the experiences we go through in life, we would not be the same people we are today. Karo: Erlend’s voice is very exposed in these songs, but the arrangements rarely try to underline every emotion he expresses. How do you decide when the music should support the voice and when it should deliberately leave it almost alone? The Sound Veil Society: It’s all about the feeling, really, and nothing we think too much about when we make music. To express ourselves the way we want, it just tends to become like that. Karo: One thing I noticed both at E-Only and on the album is how important space is. The songs are not afraid of air, pauses or sounds that are allowed to remain isolated. In electronic music, where it is technically very easy to keep adding layers, is knowing what to remove as important to you as knowing what to write? The Sound Veil Society: In a way it is, but the most important thing for us is to write a good song and express the feeling we want to express with it. We do use quite a lot of layers, but they are often subtle and just there to emphasise the sound. Since we have some years behind us making music, we have learned that sometimes less is more. Karo: The visual material often uses roads, water, landscapes, silhouettes and people partly disappearing from view. They feel less like illustrations of individual songs than fragments of memory. How closely do you work on the relationship between image and sound, and what can an image express that you deliberately leave unresolved in the lyrics? The Sound Veil Society: It depends on the idea of the song we are working on, but we often get visual ideas while making music. An image or a video clip itself is a great way to describe emotions, and combining sound and visuals simply makes a story more complete. Karo: Your musical backgrounds give you access to an established electronic vocabulary, yet “Things We Kept” does not sound interested in demonstrating genre knowledge. Was there anything from your previous projects that you consciously had to unlearn in order for The Sound Veil Society to develop its own identity? The Sound Veil Society: Not much, really. The only thing we have been trying to do is shorten parts, as it is easy to keep things simply because they sound good, but in the end they often just make a track less interesting. Other than that, everything else just fell into place during the making of it. Karo: At E-Only I had the impression that some of these songs actually became larger through performance without losing their intimacy. Has playing the material in front of people changed your understanding of the album, perhaps shown you emotional qualities in certain songs that were less obvious in the studio? The Sound Veil Society: It can happen, but we often already have an idea of how a song will work live when we make it. So most of our work is made just as much for the live stage as it is for a record, actually. Of course, before the first live show, we didn’t know how our vision would translate to the audience, but after these shows we really feel that we get a special connection with the audience. Karo: “Things We Kept” establishes a very precise emotional and visual identity for a first album. Looking ahead, does that identity now feel like a foundation you want to deepen, or something you already feel tempted to disturb? What are you curious to discover about The Sound Veil Society next? The Sound Veil Society: In a way, it is a foundation to build upon and is, in many ways, the core of our concept. But we do want to evolve and make something new along the way, so we don’t yet know what it will become. But that is also part of the fun: exploring new sides of a concept. We will always aim to be as honest and raw in our expression. About The Sound Veil Society The Sound Veil Society is a Swedish-Norwegian electronic duo formed in 2024 by Erlend Eilertsen and Hans-Olof Mattsson. Eilertsen is associated with Essence Of Mind and Lights A.M. and joined Xenturion Prime in 2024; Mattsson co-founded Code 64, later established Xenturion Prime and has also been involved with Essence Of Mind. The project debuted with “The River” on 24 April 2025, followed by “OK” on 22 August 2025 and “Hunger for Light” in March 2026. Their debut album, “Things We Kept”, was released by Progress Productions on 11 September 2026. The standard edition contains eleven tracks, including “Voices” featuring KÅRP; the CD adds three bonus versions, while the album was also issued on black-and-white splatter vinyl and as a limited MiniDisc edition. The duo performed at Nocturnal Culture Night and E-Only Festival; a live video for “Nothing to Say” was recorded at E-Only in Leipzig in March 2026. The Sound Veil Society are already confirmed for Eastside Festival in Halle (Saale), Germany, on 2-3 July 2027.
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由瑞典-挪威双人组合The Sound Veil Society创作，是他们的首张全长作品。整张唱片不以侵略性或戏剧化外放取胜，而是通过克制、留白、重复以及人声、电子声响与沉默之间精心维系的关系来累积情感重量。专辑标题"Things We Kept"随着展开逐渐显露深意——我们所留存的，往往并非主动选择保留之物，记忆、未完成的对话、过往版本的自我始终在场。专辑表面纤细，却承载着相当的力量。评论者通过现场演出与录音的对照，强调了二人将丰富阅历转化为本能的能力：经验足够时，停止展示所知，专注于歌曲真正所需。来自Progress Productions厂牌的发行，介于暗潮、电子与实验之间，以北欧冷静气质探索情感的持续性。

items.body:
This column is a loose gathering of recordings – two duos, two quartets – that might define a certain frontier, a degree of meaning in improvised interactivity spreading over 12 years. At times, the combination of close listening and simultaneous writing (the only way I can find to describe this music) results in verbal collisions that may be elusive in meaning, but they may also legitimately represent some of the transformative complexity and overlapping visions arising in these works of essentially collective invention. Though one of these recordings is more than a decade old, they may represent a kind of perpetual edge.

Certain musics can pass through walls of custom, identity, and meaning, assuming unknown shapes, escaping any strict verbal denotation, meaning becoming at once plastic and ineffable. Such music cannot be analyzed or described successfully, such failed exercises, however, perhaps contributing to both its mystery and its beauty, music that might suggest a hymn from an unknown culture, possibly disappeared, to an unknown deity, possibly deceased. In collectively improvised music, the role of the listener is paramount: assembling, collecting, composing ... At the same time, however, no interpretation is more privileged than another. These particular recordings are by musicians who can create dreams in sound. Some will imagine mills or factory floors, tuned to and amplifying unimaginable inventions of human industry. Empathy contributes a mutating, transformational soundscape. These are musics that create uncommon space.

Die Dritte Ebene (45 rpm LP, NiVuNiConnu, nvnc-lp062) by Emilio Gordoa and the late Sven-Åke Johansson might initially seem exotic. Ultimately, it’s not. It’s work of perfect transparency, that is, a view of whatever one hears as the other side of anywhere. The cover offers two titles, DIE DRITTE EBEN or EL TERCER NIVEL, “the third level,” in German or Spanish, with each phrase written with the “E”s written as reversed 3s. The phrase arises in Gordoa’s brief description appended to the Bandcamp page: “We were discussing how our music moves as if in parallel lines, and how after a while something third will emerge from it, almost like a ghost. It is something I find almost mystical: how this third level manifested itself in our playing without us thinking about it.”

Reminiscent of Johansson’s previous NiVuNiConnu release, Tea Time, with Nicholas Bussmann and Yan Jun, the music hints at Erik Satie’s Furniture Music, somehow constituting a radical background music that enhances consciousness, the special resonance of repeated materials creating a trance-like, near-ecstatic state, a reflective consciousness that rises between the parts created by Johansson and Gordoa, illuminating as well as hypnotic. Die Dritte Ebene, from August 26, 2023, points to an ineffable quality – a kind of trance, a kind of lift, a spectral point of attention that is produced in a listener’s collaboration with the close echoes, tight resonance and metallic rattle of Johansson’s snare, the reeds of his accordion, and the glassy ring of Gordoa’s vibraphone, glowing like light in sonic form. The shared insistence and simultaneity of Johansson and Gordoa’s work consistently expands what is essentially a minimalist musical environment, concluding with a strange abstraction of accordion and vibraphone that might suggest a kind of musical haunting.

Nate Wooley and Seymour Wright recorded About Trumpet and Saxophone in 2012, appearing on the Fataka label in 2013. While that release was unquestionably radical, its forthcoming successor, recorded in 2025, About Saxophone and Trumpet (Relative Pitch) takes a very different initial tack, opening with a deconstruction of the romantic ballad “The Midnight Sun,” composed by Lionel Hampton and Sonny Burke in 1947, recorded initially as an instrumental, with sufficient melodic grace to have lyrics later added by Johnny Mercer, spurring recordings by June Christy, Ella Fitzgerald, and Carmen McRae. Here the melody is clearly audible through a series of gasps, honks, and shattered, incomplete phrases, a nod to tradition that rapidly expands, becoming increasingly inclusive.

There follows “Experiment Four,” an extended dialogue which includes some of the strangest sounds ever emitted by saxophone and trumpet, often coming from very different positions in the sound spectrum. The fourth track, “Untitled,” is genuinely conversational, though the conversation is conducted in assorted bleats and blasts. Each musician is repeatedly triggered by the other’s material, whether pinching their sound inward, or adapting a radical extroversion. Music here will stand in for complex human relationships and perceptions, a sound store evolving to mark the impact of events in one’s daily life, worlds for which artists have long been refining their techniques and perceptions. As our descriptive apparatus daily fails before global events, our key artists stretch the elements. In that sense, call it modern syntactical practice or a soundtrack to Guernica, but the expressive range in which Wooley and Wright here operate seems perfectly in keeping with the daily news. Meanwhile, the inner tunings and sustained tones, even their matching fast vibratos suggest the development and synergy of an expressionist language. Sudden shifts will swiftly resemble elegant balladry of yore, echoes of that “Midnight Sun.”

While the Wooley/Wright duet recalls Fataka, Trevor Brent’s remarkable label – “‘dedicated to releasing recordings of small group and solo improvisations with a particular interest in situations where a common musical language has not yet fully emerged” – has become active again, releasing Parallels & Diagonals by a quartet from the label’s earlier period, 14th July 2014 at Cafe Oto, in which Wooley and Wright appear in a quartet with two percussionists active since the dawn of English free improvisation, Paul Lytton and Eddie Prévost. Contrary to Brent’s explanation of the label (and a genuine generational difference: the percussionists had discographies before the wind players were born), the four musicians seem so closely attuned – each a genuine spontaneous composer – that they sound like they might have had a long history together. Parallels and Diagonals is 12-year-old music, but it sounds like it might be recorded next year.

The opening track, the extended Parallel A, sounds like a machine shop that has discovered free improvisation, shifting dramatically after a passage of silence shortly after the 15-minute mark. The sounds suggest a light roll on a kettle drum, a brush on a cymbal, the sound of air pushed delicately through a trumpet. This notion of interiority marks the collective passage of these musicians, finding a terrain at once both barely imagined and yet a defining part of the human condition. In Diagonal A, fundamental gestures, like air squeezed through a metal tube, take on their own significance, behaving like Buddhist mudras, invoking fundamental gestures and symptoms of human life, murmurs, signs, abrasions. Diagonal B’s rapid actions and continuous overlapping suggest activity so closely attended by the musicians that it might follow a score in which the pauses might be carefully accounted, floating among a delicately bowed cymbal, other sounds that cannot be identified, and some that shimmer around audibility.

foam and mesh (Fundacja Słuchaj Records) by the B:A:N:S BAND is the work of pianist Sophie Agnel, saxophonist John Butcher, bassist Pascal Niggenkemper, and percussionist Ståle Liavik Solberg, recorded at the 2024 ArtAct Festival in St. Johann, Austria. While it’s the only grouping here with a conventional instrumental grouping, the orientation of the musicians will ensure that there is nothing resembling convention in the ways that the instruments are utilized.

foam and mesh I is clearly the main event, a 35-minute dialogue in which four of the most skilled spontaneous composers put together a dense weave of sonic events, with nothing predictable, yet everything interlocking. Tension curves are developed with astonishing power, each member of the quartet seemingly pursuing a unique and independent path, yet everything contributing to an astonishing rhythmic taffy-pull in which every part contribute to a compound and original overall momentum. This complex relationship will sustain through numerous group movements, whether slow balladic ruminations with isolated knocks and flurries or a sudden tense wedding of trembling oscillations, all four musicians regularly finding distinct timbres. The relatively brief foam and mesh II initially foregrounds Agnel’s piano, her focus initially on brief, isolated, tight-knit clusters with abstract flurries from Niggenkemper’s bass and the randomizing knitwork of Liavik Solberg. When Butcher initially enters on soprano saxophone, the random patterns generally coalesce into a continuous stream of different rhythms and complementary densities before the work’s ultimately gradual disappearance.

items._cn_summary: 本篇乐评聚焦于即兴音乐的'边界地带'，涵盖两组二重奏与两组四重奏录音，横跨十二年创作历程。文章探讨集体即兴中'密切聆听与同步书写'的独特互动方式，以及音乐如何超越习俗、身份与意义的界限，形成流动而难以言说的形态。评介重点提及Emilio Gordoa与已故Sven-Åke Johansson的专辑《Die Dritte Ebene》，二人以打击乐与人声/物件发声展开对话，呼应Erik Satie的'家具音乐'理念，通过重复素材的特殊共振营造恍惚、近乎出神的状态，被描述为'第三层'——从平行线条中浮现的幽灵般的第三种存在。该厂牌为瑞士小型实验厂牌NiVuNiConnu，体现典型的地下独立发行美学。

items.body:
Gerry Hemingway leads a band of globe-trotters: German multi-reedist Frank Gratkowski whose recorded in the US often; pianist Izumi Kimura based in Ireland; Swiss bassist Christian Weber who’s recorded on three continents, crossing paths along the way with Yanks Oliver Lake, Ellery Eskelin, Nate Wooley, and Russ Johnson; Gerry himself, based in Lucerne since 2009.

In many ways Hemingway’s contemporary music mines his time in Anthony Braxton’s wondrous 1985-1993 quartet. The leaping staccato melody with asymmetrical phrases near the top of the 36-minute “Bau 4 Assembly” is one marker; another, the way that loose suite and the 23-minute “Slivers” use long improvised sections to tie together occasional scored episodes – not that Braxton was alone in that. And Braxton’s quartet prompted Hemingway’s duo with bandmate Marilyn Crispell, prefiguring his duo with Kimura in recent years.

On the CD, a six-minute Hemingway-Kimura improvisation is sandwiched between the long pieces, but I tend to cue up that “Third Story Variation” first, for its unbeatable interplay. The pianist and drummer catch and ride the same pulse, leaving plenty of air but also knowing how to fill various spaces along the way. Their timbral senses are fully compatible: her under-the-hood preparations tilt her sound drumward. They’ll set up a slow groove together, then she’ll use her other hand to play against it. It’s all very attentive and effective.

The longer pieces credited to Hemingway unfold like narratives, with discreet episodes, varied pacing, subgroup subplots, ways to build and dispel tension. “Slivers” is for trio, minus piano, Gratkowski leading off on squawky bass clarinet, tracked by Weber’s bass; the time feel is notably looser than the duo’s. A few minutes in, bass clarinet exits, and Frank’s re-entrance on disembodied wispy alto is placed just right: an instant orchestrator’s decision. Later there’s a section for low bass clarinet and arco bass in frictive unison under free drum rustle – suggesting Braxton’s love of the sub-basement, and the flexible trio dynamic of Gerry’s early/longtime vehicle BassDrumBone. But “Slivers” does slack off a bit between the scored tentpoles. There are times you wish the drummer would apply a firmer hand in a what-would-Billy-Higgins-do kind of way. One of Gerry’s signatures at the traps is a free-swinging–arms sense of relaxation, hitting the skins as if on the rebound, with some hits maybe dropped or delayed in transit. In the closing minutes, and on the closing theme, he can come off like someone who thinks he’s swinging harder than he is.

All four assemble for “Bau 4 Assembly” which makes up the bulk of the program. The venue Bau 4 in Altbüron, Switzerland was founded by folks in the timber business, and is located in their commercial compound. In tribute, Gerry and company play or use as beaters wood scraps retrieved from the workshop, notably heard around 10 minutes in, on a fast irregular clacky and texturally light colloquy which develops into something like pointillism with a groove (no small achievement) before flute and pedal-down piano soften things up. But not for long; in very short order, a scrapwood and piano gamelan. Midway, there’s a long-tone chapter with clarinet, and Gerry singing wavery lines into his cymbals or (says here) through metal objects, an odd effect he just about pulls off. (There’s a little Robert Wyatt in his vocal wah-wahs.) The composer and the quartet cover much ground. Elsewhere, a slow line’s melodic contours are subtly mirrored by the drums.

We won’t catalog every change-up or chapter, but near the end there’s a free-jazz blowout whose presence feels like checking a box – which is not to overlook Frank’s rapid multiphonic growls. (He’s got a great command of altissimo and pressurized reed textures.) Then they break into a loose brisk tempo, to frame that free-jazz energy. It arrives just where a non-drummer’s band would place a climactic the drum solo. Then a feint toward the Braxtonian head from half an hour earlier. A few staccato hits end things without a big fuss.

items._cn_summary: 这张现场专辑由鼓手Gerry Hemingway领衔，集合了德国次中音/高音萨克斯手Frank Gratkowski、爱尔兰钢琴家Izumi Kimura和瑞士贝斯手Christian Weber四位跨国乐手。专辑受Anthony Braxton四重奏影响深远，以长篇组曲形式展开叙事：36分钟的《Bau 4 Assembly》和23分钟的《Slivers》通过即兴段落串联零散的有谱段落，呈现松散套曲结构。Kimura在钢琴内部使用预置物件，使音色向鼓的质感靠拢，与Hemingway形成脉动一致的低保真双人对话。《Slivers》中Gratkowski以低音单簧管和悬浮的高音萨克斯交替主导，揭示出编排层面的精心考量。《Bau 4 Assembly》亮点在于用从瑞士Altbüron Bau4木材厂拾得的木块作为打击发声器，融入了场地自身的历史质感。Hemingway自由摆荡的鼓风贯穿始终，但在曲中段略有松散之嫌。

items.body: Josh Mason’s L+ marks the second to last release for the Dauw label for 2018. In the ‘About’ section of his website, Mason talks about working ‘ in different processing environments’ and although he is talking about the tools to make the sounds, Mason’s compositions in L+ do feel like he is creating environments for his melodies to inhabit. L+ opens into existence with a modulated sound, slowly undulating. Quickly from that single sound branches off three or four strands of sound that are then drawn back into it, to be re-immersed. But that core sound that brought the piece still lives on, underneath it all. And this is where the notion of creating audio environments is a useful lens to view L+’s compositions – it’s as if Mason is defining the piece of land or territory where his sonic strands will live. And this is one of the repeated techniques on L+: most pieces start with a sound that remains the foundation for the duration of the piece. Also typical of L+ is those sonic/musical strands that exist on or against the backdrop of sonic land that Mason creates for each composition. They often present themselves as glitches – microcosms of sound – that simply burst into existence and move along. None of those strands of sound really comes together, but nothing really runs counter to any of the other sounds at play. It’s as if Mason sends his players in motion but bounds them – they can go where they may and interact as they will, but they all exist within a sort of fenced-in confines. And the real magic is in the way those strands overlay or inhabit the space of that core sound upon which they exist. Across the 6 pieces of L+ Mason plays with that formula and, interestingly, L+ almost becomes more minimal as it proceeds. It’s as if by slowing things down, yes, things sound a little glitchier and we are closer to the mechanics of the compositions, and still, somehow, they become more immersive. In some cases, the composition’s move so slow, those strands of sound almost literally sound like electricity moving across a a wire. Of the album Mason writes: “I had seneca’s letters on ethics and epictetus’ enchiridion right next to me. as i considered the choices i was making with the sounds you hear, i was also pausing to have a think on the things i was reading. each track corresponds with some maxim found in either copy i had of each book (ie S26 = seneca, pg. 26.) the first piece and last piece are based on a two part axiom, and so both pieces are connected sonically in some ways, as two ends of a piece of tape might be spliced together.” Ambient/minimal electronic music as philosophy is interesting territory because there is something to be said for the broad philosophy that ambient music asks us to slow down in an ever quickening world. But what Mason is talking about is a bit different, in that he is taking the treatises and tracts of other thinkers and basing his sounds around their ideas to create sound explorations or meditations of their philosophies and put those ideas into sonic motion. My first note when starting to write my review of L+ was to write “ Can an album be welcoming without first being inviting?”. The coarse aspects of those glitchy components seemed, objectively speaking, abrasive – even against their seemingly subdued backdrops. But, once immersed, everything about L+ feels full and, yes, inviting even. In the world of L+ sounds pop, crackle, hiss, undulate, vibrate, wave, disintegrate, flicker, and feel sometimes random, but there is no entropy – there are entire worlds at play in each composition. L+ is a sublime collection of minimal electronic music that nicely wraps up 2018. L+ by Josh Mason www.dauw.bandcamp.com

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以极简电子手法构建声音环境，每首作品都从一种核心音色出发，逐渐生长出若干声音支线，但始终围绕那块'声音领地'运行。Josh Mason采用缓慢调制与微粒化声音处理，使旋律碎片如同电流沿导线移动，呈现出愈发沉浸的聆听体验。整体走向随专辑推进愈加克制和极简，从缓慢的进程中将声音的机械结构暴露于听者面前。作为哲学冥想式的声音探索，每首曲目对应斯多葛学派哲学家塞涅卡与爱比克泰德著作中的一则格言，首尾两曲更基于同一公理的两部分，在声学层面相互呼应，形成首尾相接的整体。

items.body: While the ambient music subgenre of field recording has already been heavily explored, there is a renewing naivete I find in layering protoconversation and young children’s laughs and chatter onto monoid synth. While children can come out with the most random question of reality at uncertain times, monoid synth drone matching with vocals is something still refreshing and wonderful. The happy/sad neutralising is enigmatic. ‘Field Recording Meets Sound’ is a superb exploration of the will ‘o wisp burn of good ambience in a post-youthquake environment of milleni-mania. The sleepy-eyed and toxic nature of drone impregnates the surface sheen of the quality dorian-led sounds, and the nascent lack of solidified scales lends the music a naively posited professionalism, hence a between-state, a purity of fashion. The opening to the record conjures up a bustling city street, cars passing and humans moving bumper to bumper of the drone’s base-line. There is a cordial overlap between choral music and musique concrete; voice shards blend into a smoothie mush against the very Pausal and Rafael Antoni Irissari esque hum of the record. Meaning to placate emotionally the roundabout encirclement of the somehow managed vocal loops, there is a majesty of tapestry coagulated through forceful re-clustering of the central vocal/synth sound set. A gripping element of the music is its immediate joility and then its spreading of aesthetic colours into a peacock tail kaleidoscope of sometimes languid, occasionally touching and regularly haunting passages. What particularly excites and succeeds about this album is its candour. It sounds innocent. Always of its time; never pretentious. These feelings you get channeled from the drones are contentment based. Recommended! www.krysalisound.com
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将田野录音与合成器嗡鸣融为一体，使用儿童对话、笑声与人群喧嚣作为主要素材层叠在单音合成器持续音之上。创作者将协唱与具象音乐并置处理，嗓音碎片被打散混入底层的嗡鸣之中，形成一种边界模糊的织体结构。评论者特别提到音乐中快乐与悲伤相互中和的张力，以及开场部分模拟城市街景的车流与人声如何在嗡鸣基线之上展开。全作呈现出一种朴素的诚实感，既不属于当下流行话语，也并非刻意先锋，而是以一种近乎纯真的方式处理声音材料。专辑融合了田野录音特有的环境真实感与电子嗡鸣的抽象质地，两者之间的对话构成核心聆听体验。

items.body: “I was interested in distress sounds, sirens, flares, etc,” reads a peculiar passage from the press junket for Jake Marshall’s debut album. Quite humorously, the same statement could double as surplus copy for Her Majesty’s Coastguard. The London-based musician and visual artist’s exploratory first release, Fresh Water, features eight tracks themed around motifs of emergency and crisis. With a conceptual arc starring repurposed survival signals, one might forecast a cyclone worthy of striking scurvy into the heartiest sea-wizened veteran. Instead, Marshall’s Fresh Water thrills with rhythmic revelations, inducing sonic mirages along the way. Whether shipwrecked or just plain lost, survival calls have served a single purpose throughout history: When facing threat to life or limb, one must make a visible or audible signal which will draw immediate attention. Quite tellingly, blaring alarms initiate Fresh Water: a quartet of sirens sizzle in mid- and hi-frequencies throughout “P5ws.” Woven together sparingly, frayed horns pulse in binary hysteria as synthetic strings shudder beneath. Directed by a drum beat ricocheting down dub hallways, “Forgo” bristles with elongated notes trembling in monotone to the image of a lonely flare sinking slowly underwater. Looped into modulated motifs akin to a minimalist composer with an ear for Krautrock, the sirens return on “Grid,” ear-piercing and chest-rattling, throbbing for spine-tingling miles. “Jan 1” opens with a celestial transmission: squelching feedback spins in limbo across ham radio frequencies; ghostly harmonics arouse the stereo field to a mild melody light enough to catch a breeze—or a cold. “Thro” ignites its twilight signal on the deck of the stranded cargo ship. But the search boat’s probing lights sweep right by, oblivious to the blazing oil barrel shrouded by fog. Now try to get some sleep. Fatigue setting in, Fresh Water’s title track revives the remaining survivors with club-ready sirens. Cycling up and down frenetic scales, white light from a high intensity strobe machine pulses vigorously on a dance floor driven by 4/4 beats. Cast in the nimbus of neon glow sticks, the mid-track lull blurs into an elfin trill: woozy like a Wurlitzer high on helium. A fluttering flute descends, fending off flies: wah-wah’d notes washed by an oblivion of pitch-shifted keys. As the helicopters circle nearby, keep both arms outstretched—raising and lowering them repeatedly. “Like A Mothers Love” exudes little assurance in said patrimonial affection. A vaguely Middle-Eastern melody pushes through static, liquefying into the skipping bass of a fog horn. Other accoutrements gradually festoon the proceedings: a sonic ritual forms around the raising of a maritime flag; hollow synths float steadily behind a constellation of electronic clamoring; a bobbing bass line, punctuated by hollow wood blocks, carries a Morse code transmission into heat-craze and hunger. Apply sunscreen liberally. “Outro” introduces resignation onto the lone life raft. Ruffled waves nudge the rubber boat sideways, the microphone crackling with an indifferent wind. As the stranded oil tanker slumps into the water: cavernous explosions boom alongside handguns fired overhead. A solemn synth tapers towards blackout, reaching for rations and reasons. Leery that the nearing helicopter may be merely a hallucination, the sole survivor casts dye markers overboard—just to be safe. The search team hovers on the horizon as lazy waves guide a pool of green dye starboard: drifting away from the raft, pulling towards a final hope. Although not without aquatic dangers, Fresh Water graciously negates the possibility of death by drowning or predation. Playfully buoyant and brightly colored, there is no need to measure Fresh Water’s salinity. And yet the absence of salt is no guarantee that sun or wave might not still maim. When sailing through Fresh Water, make sure to pack those suede shoes with a polyester vest. Only cinch the life jacket snugly, and hurl the preserver wide when Jake Marshall is on duty. items._cn_summary: Jake Marshall首张专辑《Fresh Water》以八首作品构建了一套围绕求救信号、警报与海上遇难的听觉叙事。创作者将警报声、喇叭鸣响、无线电反馈、合成器弦乐等素材编织成节奏化的音景，在dub式鼓点与4/4舞曲律动之间切换，既有极简主义作曲家的循环动机，也带有Krautrock的推进感。中段标题曲转向俱乐部化处理，闪烁的失谐笛音与俯仰调制键盘形成迷幻效果。专辑在中东旋律片段、莫尔斯电码节奏与海洋雾气般的电子质感之间穿行，整体呈现出概念完整、声音设计精细的实验电子拼贴美学，适合对声音叙事与场域化聆听有兴趣的听众。
