items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是内罗毕新厂牌Cool Waters的首发作品，由德国出生的肯尼亚打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo组成的二人组Odd Okoddo，携手八十三岁的肯尼亚传统dodo歌唱家Ogoya Nengo共同完成。音乐以Kacirek的Buchla合成器、手掌打击乐与偶尔的架子鼓构建电子律动底色，承载两位歌手的声线交织。文中重点分析的《Bara》展示了从廉价打击声逐步叠加4/4节拍、低音与木琴音色的层积过程，合成多节奏以几乎不易察觉的细腻方式浮现，最终与歌声融为一体。《Sarah》则以Ratengo的主唱配合Kacirek试探性的打击碎片与尖锐失真，凸显紧张感。乐评将这类跨文化创作置于更广阔语境中，与Chouk Bwa及Nyege Nyege厂牌的作品相提并论，指出其核心在于文化间的真诚对话而非猎奇拼贴，使传统根源在电子语境中重新获得前卫感。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由Dorothy Moskowitz与作曲家Francesco Paolo Paladino及诗人Luca Chino Ferrari合作完成，收录十一首歌曲。音乐以钢琴为核心，穿插弦乐、木管与合成器音色，呈现非线性、模态化的结构特征，刻意打破西方传统和声逻辑的束缚。评论将其与Steve Reich、Philip Glass的简约主义传统相联系，认为作品在解构歌曲形式的同时拓展了更古老、更遥远的声音叙事。歌词层面充满政治隐喻与社会批判，《Pale Wanderer》讨论极权主义的共谋结构，《Charlottesville》则直面当代法西斯主义的威胁，同时融入对死亡与人类存在位置的哲学沉思。Moskowitz的演唱如同方法派演员，将每个词的重量置于旋律之上，钢琴既是人声延伸也是评论式的希腊合唱，独立厂牌Silentes发行，整体定位介于先锋音乐与诗歌之间。

items._cn_summary: 这张九碟套装系统梳理了韩裔美国作曲家及伽倻琴演奏家金熙（Kim Jin Hi）的创作脉络，涵盖管弦乐与室内乐作品，并收录她与Susie Ibarra、Derek Bailey、Tony Oxley、Oliver Lake、William Parker等即兴高手的合作录音。评论聚焦五张代表性专辑，呈现传统韩国乐器与西方自由即兴、前卫作曲之间的对话与张力。五十二首曲目横跨多种编制，既有学院派作曲的严谨结构，也有即兴演奏的开放探索。整体而言，这套合集为理解金熙的跨文化创作提供了较完整的入口，适合对当代音乐与即兴场景交叉领域感兴趣的听众深入研究。

items.body: A centuries-old devotional song from Morocco’s Gnawa repertoire, “M’Bara Meskin” tells of poor M’Bara, left outside the shrine in torn clothes to brew his tea from leaves others have thrown away. Inside, the Sidi and the Lalla, Moroccan honorifics for a gentleman and a lady, sip theirs in their slippers. Sydney-born multi-instrumentalist Julian Belbachir has rebuilt it on reggae and dub, keeping the vocal in Moroccan Arabic, from sessions in Morocco, Mali, Australia, Canada and Jamaica. Belbachir was born to a Moroccan father and an Australian mother and grew up in Surry Hills and Redfern, where he started on West African drums at five under griots and master drummers from Sydney’s African diaspora. He went on to study percussion and instrument-making in Guinea, Senegal, Mali and Morocco, and plays the kamele n’goni, the harp-lute of Mali’s Wassoulou region. From 2013 to 2022 he drummed for the Australian Indigenous dub band OKA, and after the death of its founder, Stuart “Boga” Fergie, he went solo with his 2022 debut album, Babdoukkala. Gnawa music was carried into Morocco by West Africans brought north across the Sahara, many of them enslaved, and the personnel on his forthcoming album, The Golden Light, follow the same route: more than 30 musicians from Mali and Morocco, among them Moussa Diakite, lead guitarist for Salif Keita. “M’Bara Meskin” came out on 11 September as its first single, with the album due in February 2027. Belbachir hears the song as a portrait of “the hardships musicians face in their daily lives“. The video, shot on Super 8 over two trips to Essaouira three years apart, follows his collaborators through rehearsals, recording sessions and time with their community in the Atlantic port best known for its annual Gnawa festival. Hear “M’Bara Meskin” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Julian Belbachir – M’Bara Meskin appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._genre: Gnawa / reggae / dub / world fusion / African diaspora
items._cn_summary: Julian Belbachir 是来自悉尼的多乐器演奏家，摩洛哥与澳大利亚双重文化背景令他自幼接触西非鼓乐传统，后赴几内亚、塞内加尔、马里、摩洛哥深造打击乐与乐器制作，并演奏马里 Wassoulou 地区的竖琴琴 kamele n'goni。专辑《The Golden Light》以 Gnawa 传统圣歌为根基，将摩洛哥阿拉伯语人声与雷鬼、dub 节奏重构，录音跨越摩洛哥、马里、澳大利亚、加拿大与牙买加。参与阵容超过三十位音乐人，包括 Salif Keita 的首席吉他手 Moussa Diakite。首支单曲《M'Bara Meskin》讲述贫穷朝圣者被拒于神庙之外、以他人弃茶为饮的故事，Belbachir 将其视为音乐人日常困苦的肖像。MV 以 Super 8 胶片在索维拉分两次拍摄，记录排练、录音及社群生活，呼应 Gnawa 横跨撒哈拉的音乐迁徙脉络。

items.body: The German duo Grimoire De Occulte has been active for several years now and has released the majority of its work, particularly in recent years. Inspired by Bernd Hermanns, aka ‘Baal’ (owner of Dunkelheit Produktionen and also active in several other projects), and ‘Philosoph’, they originally released this album in 2025, with the CD version following this year. The title word ‘Ajna’ undoubtedly refers to the Sanskrit word usually translated as ‘perceiving’, ‘knowing’, or ‘insight’. It also represents the sixth chakra, which is associated with the so-called third eye. This aligns perfectly with the approach of this project, which has always been closely linked to ritual and mysticism. We are presented with an elaborate and unique track lasting nearly 40 minutes. “Ajna: Transmissions” invites the listener to immerse themselves in an esoteric world in which the ‘other side’ plays a prominent role. This naturally provides inspiration for a dark composition, with the duo presenting us with a persistent, ominous wave of sound. At first glance, it may seem somewhat monotonous, yet the composition is enriched with humming sound effects and additional sounds, including all kinds of crackling field recordings. The whole piece is also punctuated by a scream, which adds extra power to the dark ritual. As far as I’m concerned, a few additional tracks could have been included here, but this extended “Ajna: Transmissions” remains a pleasant listen nonetheless. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Anja: Transmissions”: https://dunkelheitprod.bandcamp.com/track/ajna-transmissions
items._cn_summary: 德国二人组 Grimoire De Occulte 发行了近40分钟的单一长篇作品，标题 Ajna 取自梵语，象征第三眼与内观智慧，与该项目一贯的仪式与神秘主义主题相契合。整首作品以持续的低沉暗流声波为主干，铺陈出浓厚的黑暗仪式氛围，中间穿插嗡鸣音效与各种噼啪作响的田野录音，并被一声尖叫所打断，为作品增添了仪式感与冲击力。乐评指出作品初听略显单调，但细腻的声音层次弥补了结构上的不足，同时认为若能增加额外曲目会使整体更完整。整体而言，这是一张在暗潮与仪式音乐领域内具有专注探索精神的专辑，适合沉浸式聆听。

items.body: Fawning, we’re brighter, we’re cautious, Falling like fighters, we’re caustic. Cracked up like actors, we’re lying. Daydreams and nightmares. Sharing cigarettes and leather trousers can feel like a promising start to eternity, until eternity begins to resemble an argument neither person can leave. Berlin’s Night Nail take that unhappy prospect to the dance floor on Vile Train, a gothic rock seduction in which two lovers become so absorbed in each other that escape begins to seem as impossible as happiness. The attraction is considerable; so is the damage. The song previews Infinite Fountain, Night Nail’s fourth studio album, due November 6, 2026, through Icy Cold Records. Its accompanying video reunites the band with director and editor Jean De Oliviera, whose previous collaborations include Hollow Day, Little Armenia, and Narcoleptic Dream Catcher. Vile Train begins with a noise suspended somewhere between a buzz and a screech, while cold guitar tones gather around it with considerable menace. The drums establish their footing before a heavier, sustained riff saws through the opening, its melody making the abrasion strangely inviting. Around the thirty-second mark, the bass enters with a deep, brooding groove, and the guitar shifts into a lower, more resonant register. That change gives the song a mournful richness, setting the scene for Brandon Robert’s dark, swaggering delivery. Repeating synth figures tighten the tension beneath his voice, and roughly a minute in, the chorus sends the arrangement into a more urgent gothic dance beat. The construction is remarkably assured: each entrance increases the pressure, while the bass keeps enough melodic independence to make the groove feel alive. By the three-minute mark, its intricate phrasing has become a hook in its own right, moving beneath Robert’s breathy repetition of “Daydreams and nightmares” as a feminine voice echoes the words in whispers. The song’s pleasure comes from those relationships between the instruments, the way an ominous opening develops into something so physically persuasive. Robert found the initial inspiration during a visit to Pompeii, where a fresco depicting an angel and a demon in an embrace suggested a romance with a particularly poor prognosis. In the song’s conception, two dreamers inhabit separate modern realities until their fantasies bring them together. They exchange clothes, cigarettes, and intimacies, gradually making a prison of the connection that first seemed to offer freedom. Robert describes the result as “dark and brutal truths about love sung in a twisted but beautiful way.” The lyrics give that deterioration a nasty intimacy. Caution sits beside fawning, attraction beside aggression, and the lovers seem increasingly aware of the roles they have been playing. “Some days I wish I was her” carries the confusion further, towards the point where wanting another person begins to erase the distinction between their identity and your own. Against the recurring admission of lies, the fantasy of America offers another possible elsewhere. Every imagined exit seems to lead back to the same two people. Vile Train was mixed and post-produced by William Faith at 13 Studio in Chicago, with co-production by Night Nail in Berlin and additional vocals and guitar from VV & the Void. That combination serves a song whose writing and arrangement make its gothic excess feel earned, with a chorus capable of turning private misery into a crowded dance floor. Directed and edited by Jean De Oliviera, the video gives Vile Train a stark black-and-white treatment, cutting between Robert and bassist Ilija Gavrilenko performing among amplifiers and outdoor shots framed by stone arches and fountain basins. Black leather, dark glasses, and severe makeup give the pair a suitably funereal glamour, while tight shots of fingers on strings bring the song’s instrumental interplay into focus. Robert’s face repeatedly fills the frame, his dark lipstick and pale features isolated against the black background. Grain, scratches, and superimposed silhouettes of reaching hands disturb that severe simplicity, spreading across faces and instruments until the musicians seem caught behind the image itself. Robert’s own gestures towards the lens make the camera feel uncomfortably close, turning performance into something between an invitation and an accusation. The recurring close-ups and grasping hands give the song’s obsession a physical form, suggesting an intimacy that has become impossible to escape. It is an effective visual rendering of what the band calls the “afterlife of relationship hell,” where the desire to hold someone close has acquired a distinctly claustrophobic meaning. Watch the video for Vile Train below: Formed in Los Angeles in 2013, Night Nail relocated to Berlin in 2018, the year their debut album LA Demons appeared on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed through Cold Transmission in 2020, with Fates Explained arriving on Metropolis Records in 2023. The archival release Early Demons and Demos and remix album Fates Remade followed in 2024. Their earlier work with producer Pete Burns of Kill Shelter helped establish a catalogue that connects darkwave electronics with gothic rock’s appetite for emotional extremes. Infinite Fountain also includes mixing and post-production work by Sven Wolff of Patenbrigade: Wolff. Night Nail plans to support the album with shows across the US, UK, and Europe during 2026–2027. In the meantime, explore their back catalog on Bandcamp. Follow Night Nail: Bandcamp Spotify Facebook Instagram YouTube Website The post “Daydreams and Nightmares” — Night Nail Turns Desire Into Damnation in Video for “Vile Train” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: Night Nail 的这首单曲以哥特摇滚为骨架，将黑暗的浪漫叙事推至舞池。歌曲以介于嗡鸣与尖啸之间的噪音开场，冷峻的吉他音色层层堆叠，贝斯在第三十秒进入，带来深沉的低音律动，随后合成器线条收紧张力，副歌部分转入更急促的哥特舞曲节拍。词作者在庞贝古城见到天使与恶魔相拥的壁画后获得灵感，由此构思出两位做梦者交换衣物、亲密关系与身份边界逐渐消融的故事。歌词以亲密而残酷的笔触呈现欲望如何演变为牢笼，演唱者形容作品旨在以扭曲而美丽的旋律诉说爱的黑暗真相。编曲层次清晰，各乐器的进入不断累积压迫感，贝斯保持独立的旋律走向，使整体律动充满生命力。

items.body: As you are likely well aware, this week marks the 100th anniversary of John Coltrane's birth and writers and friends of the Free Jazz Blog were asked to contribute their personal thoughts on his music and influence. The parameters for the contributions were loose, only that it should be something personal and if it so happened that an album appeared more than once, that was fine, as what it meant to the writer was surely different. We ended up with our biggest feature ever! For the next two weeks we will be featuring reflections, reviews, and anecdotes about Coltrane and his groundbreaking music. We begin today an introduction from Sammy Stein. Enjoy! Paul Acquaro John Coltrane. Src: wikipedia By Sammy Stein FJC is celebrating John Coltrane’s 100 th year. For anyone unfamiliar with his music, the following offers a brief overview of why Coltrane is ranked amongst the greatest of musicians. Through his approach, style, delivery, and unmistakable sound, Coltrane powered through the door that Ornette Coleman and others had left ajar, revealing jazz’s powerful, emotive, and transformational heart. Nothing post-Coltrane is untouched by his influence. His was not a deliberate subversion of traditional jazz, but an uncalculated stream of events, personal, spiritual, and historical, that converged in a confluence that formed his music. Coltrane’s mother bought him a saxophone when he was sixteen, and he was influenced by players including Illinois Jacquet. His grandparents were ordained ministers, his parents met through the church, and Coltrane grew up influenced by religion. He chose a different path – that of music and was not discouraged by family, yet later in his life, it was God who helped him save his music and career. Without his spiritual reawakening, Coltrane’s career may have faded. Early on, he was supported by musicians who recognised his prodigious talent. However, he became addicted to drugs and would arrive for gigs unshaven and in smelly, wrinkled clothes. He might fall asleep on stage. Miles Davis fired him, and Dizzy Gillespie didn’t follow suit only because of their friendship and his respect for Coltrane’s talent. At the nadir of his life, Coltrane reached out to God. He described a revelation he had when God spoke to him, and he set about composing exquisite music, praising God and teaching his followers. He said, “My goal is to live the truly religious life and express it through my music. If you can live it, there’s no problem about the music, because it’s part of the whole thing.” Coltrane’s first wife, Naima, was central to his early spiritual journey. A practicing Muslim, she helped him understand God’s presence in their lives. With her support, he overcame addiction within a year. His second wife, Alice, became his spiritual partner and musical collaborator. A pianist and harpist, she understood Coltrane’s desire to contribute to a greater purpose through music. Some of Coltrane’s music has an intangible quality. He understood the spiritual and temporal worlds, and his music fused the two, expressing deep spiritual inquiry alongside the mortal complexities of personality. Jazz became a place where the human condition could be expressed with unflinching honesty and transcendent beauty. Coltrane was playing at a time when conditions were ripe for rebellion and change, and he was profoundly affected by events of his time, especially the civil rights movement, initially siding with Malcolm X before aligning with Martin Luther King Jr’s belief in peaceful but persistent protest. He performed eight benefit concerts to support Martin Luther King Jr’s cause. His music channeled anger at racism and discrimination, despair at humanity’s darkness, and the beauty of praise and worship. He had faced the demons of addiction and won, and his music reflected beauty, was personal yet spoke to millions. The murder of four African American girls in the KKK bombing in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1963 profoundly affected Coltrane. Two months after the event, he took McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones into Rudy Van Gelder's studio and recorded ‘Alabama’, later released on the album Live At Birdland (Impulse 1964). As discontent rose, Coltrane’s modal technique challenged preconceived ideas about traditional jazz. Under his and other musicians’ tenure, jazz, ever the mirror of society, became more dissonant and unruly. Coltrane’s music is as relevant today as it was in the 1960s. The messages are clearly and profoundly expressed and cut to the core impulses of humanity. Because of his uncloaked humanity, listening to Coltrane feels as emergent and alive for someone encountering the music today as it did to listeners forty years, or ten years ago. Coltrane’s near-mythical status was helped by the Blue Note label, which signed Coltrane and other players, seen as risky at the time, and some iconic images, notably photographs by Francis Wolff, a skilled photographer and executive of Blue Note. Of over 33,000 pictures Wolff took (probably more), his images of John Coltrane in moments of intense concentration or creativity seem to capture the musician's essence. One of Coltrane’s gifts was his ability to perform as a soloist or as part of an ensemble. Pieces like Davis’s’ ‘Milestones’ with ‘Cannonball’ Adderley (alto sax) and Coltrane (tenor sax) responding to Davis’s trumpet with twists and turns within the original mode laid a template for modal playing (try also Coltrane's’ Spiral’ and ‘Naima’ from Giant Steps (Atlantic 1959)). Modal jazz led away from traditional jazz and toward free jazz. Free playing was where Coltrane was headed. In the 1960s, some journalists described early free jazz as a poison to jazz, and Downbeat critics described Coltrane and Dolphy’s playing as ‘nihilistic exercises’ and ‘anti-jazz.’ Miles Davis found free jazz difficult to embrace initially. However, a few years later Davis, like Coltrane and others, found free jazz liberating. Coltrane, like many free-playing musicians, connected the evolution of the music with a deepening of self-realization and the strengthening and expression of their beliefs. Alongside fellow musicians Yusef Lateef, Sonny Rollins, and others, Coltrane pursued musical mastery and self-realization. In his suite A Love Supreme (Impulse, 1965), Coltrane expressed his love and awe of God, and the final movement is based on a devotional poem he wrote. He studied different religions and philosophies, including the Indian philosophy of Jiddu Krishnamurti, which he was introduced to by Bill Evans. Coltrane perhaps expressed his love for God most during his free playing. His tracks ‘Love’ and ‘The Father, And The Son And the Holy Ghost’ on Meditations (Impulse 1965), albums Ascension (Impulse 1966), Om (Impulse, recorded 1965, released 1966), and ‘Peace on Earth’ from Infinity (Impulse, recorded 1966, released 1972), reflect his beliefs. Coltrane used the ferocity of his playing and complex techniques as a way of worship. He said he created music for God and others and wanted to be the opposing force to evil. Even those unaware of his driving beliefs find something special, untouchable, and unique in his music. Coltrane, Art Blakey, Yusef Lateef, and other musicians became part of the Ahmadiyya sect of Islam, which forbids the intake of drugs and alcohol. Coltrane said, "My music is the spiritual expression of what I am - my faith, my knowledge, my being. When you begin to see the possibilities of music, you desire to do something really good for people, to help humanity free itself from its hang-ups…I want to speak to their souls.” Some found Coltrane’s later music, with its contradictions and unresolved transitions, less pure than his earlier recordings, but for many, they remain some of the best work produced by any jazz musician. Two weeks before his death, Coltrane discussed opening a music venue without alcohol as he realized this had masked his creativity. After Coltrane died in 1967, aged just forty, Alice kept pushing musical boundaries, and her music took on a profoundly spiritual element. She collaborated with Ornette Coleman, Pharoah Sanders, and many others, and her music traversed from blues-infused melodies to unfathomable sonic journeys, but it was beautiful, and her talent won armies of devotees, so, partly through Alice, Coltrane’s legacy remained. Also through his sons. John Jr, Ravi, and Oranyan. Oranyan started playing jazz with his brothers but has gone into trance and electronic music production. John Jr was a promising bassist but was killed in a car accident when he was 17, and Ravi is a jazz musician. Alice’s grandnephew, Steven Ellison, AKA Flying Lotus, is a record label owner, producer, rapper, and DJ. Many of his recordings feature jazz samples. Coltrane’s music and persona continue to influence music and musicians. From those who followed directly, including Pharoah Sanders, Lonnie Liston, Sun Ra, Don Cherry, and John McLaughlin, to nearly every jazz musician today. In 2016,’ Alabama’ was included in John DeJohnette's 2016 album In Movement (ECM), and on this recording, sons of the original artists, including saxophonist Ravi Coltrane (son of Coltrane) and bassist Matthew Garrison (son of bassist Jimmy Garrison), played. Coltrane’s music has been sampled on recordings by hip hop artists, younger jazz musicians, and many others. FJC is celebrating the fact that Coltrane left his influence, and there are some great pieces following this introduction. It is impossible to adequately record the influence of John Coltrane on the music that followed, but we can try. As a jazz musician recently said to me, ‘Don’t worry, just stick on some ‘Trane.” Perhaps more than any other jazz musician, John Coltrane showed there is a way to play from the heart without constraints. When you can do that, you allow your true spirit to reveal itself. Like ‘Trane. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: (Photo credit: Allen Cohen) Reaching Marlboro requires a gradual surrender of scale. Roads narrow, familiar coordinates loosen, and the forest exerts its own editorial influence, stripping away whatever feels extraneous until distance becomes a form of concentration. On September 20, 2026, that concentration gathered inside Ragle Hall at the Serkin Center, where the Marlboro Music Artist Residency Program presented The World of György Kurtág, an arresting sequence of works composed or arranged for soprano and double bass. Beyond the hall stood the wooded seclusion of southern Vermont; within it, soprano Lucy Fitz Gibbon and bassist William Langlie Miletich moved between Sprechstimme, art song, extended technique, and charged silence. Seclusion mattered because Kurtág’s music alters the proportions of attention. The claim embedded in the program’s title was stranger than its apparent simplicity suggested. The phrase “world of” ordinarily announces breadth, an oeuvre surveyed from above. Kurtág offers no such cartographic comfort. His world emerges through radical compression, forming under pressure between a sound and its possible disappearance. A few pitches can contain the moral weight of a dramatic scene. A pause can bend duration until time folds inward, secreting another time inside itself. His miniatures remain small only to the clock. To enter them is to accept unfamiliar laws under which fragments carry the mass of vanished wholes and inhalation behaves as active matter. The surrounding forest supplied an uncannily precise grammar for this experience. Every trunk concealed years in concentric script; every root continued a sentence underground. Kurtág’s art operates within a related economy of the imperceptible. A phrase ends, yet its pressure travels elsewhere. Music becomes the audible extremity of processes occurring beneath language. The sequence approached that hidden economy gently through Lembit Beecher’s With Grandchildren, drawn from his 2014 cycle Looking at Spring: Meditations on Aging. The larger work grew from interviews librettist Liza Balkan conducted with senior citizens in Toronto and central Vermont, making its appearance in Marlboro feel almost homeward. Their voices had passed into text and music before returning to the region transformed, bearing traces of their speakers without claiming to preserve them intact. Harmonics in the bass courted a rocking motion whose comfort never became secure, while Fitz Gibbon searched amid the delicate failures of memory. The soul became an unfinished sentence poised beneath scissors, family albums reduced to particles of touch and chronology. Bone creaked as marrow acquired a secret literacy, becoming a divining instrument for the inaccessible past. Beecher respected recollection as an unstable act in which forgetting shapes experience as decisively as retention. Miletich’s pale overtones gave the bass an elderly nervous system of its own. The final word escaped capture, suspending language where recognition touches disappearance. John Cage’s The Wonderful Widow of Eighteen Springs opened another passage into that borderland. Composed in 1942, its text comes from a nocturnal passage concerning Isobel in Finnegans Wake, a book of sleeping consciousness and linguistic mutation. Cage answered that abundance with severe economy. The voice circles within three pitches, while the original accompaniment is played on a closed piano tapped by the player. In Marlboro, those impulses migrated to the double bass, where Miletich turned his instrument of choice into a hollow nocturnal chamber. What had once been struck wood surrounding dormant strings now came from an assemblage held against the player’s body, each impact becoming a coded knock from somewhere inside itself. Fitz Gibbon sustained Cage’s narrow compass with remarkable intensity. Repetition wandered in place, circling a road inferred from every failed attempt to leave it. James Joyce’s words acquired the phosphorescence of objects glimpsed among trees. Isobel became a consciousness translated into the landscape, as identity passed into leaf matter and the boundary between a sleeping mind and the forest dreaming it lost authority. Amy Beth Kirsten’s yes I said yes I will Yes followed as a second excavation of Joyce, drawing on Molly Bloom’s concluding monologue in Ulysses. Written in 2012 for soprano and contrabass, with the bassist also vocalizing, it entered an illuminating dialogue with Cage. Both composers extract a concentrated vocal world from Joyce’s literary machinery. Whereas Cage cools language toward incantation, Kirsten restores its heat while fracturing the body that generates it. Isobel’s suspension yields to Molly’s consciousness in bed, where memory moves through eros and resistance before reaching the irrevocable “Yes.” Fitz Gibbon and Miletich rendered that sensuality as a condition divided against itself. Pizzicato entered beside Miletich’s droning hum, while glissandi bent the music from stable coordinates. Fitz Gibbon inhabited desire while observing its mechanisms from afar, consciousness hovering above its own flesh. The deeply inflected conclusion unfolded as slow-motion blues, each pitch bearing the drag of pleasure becoming memory before experience could have its say. These works prepared the ear for Kurtág’s Einige Sätze aus den Sudelbüchern Georg Christoph Lichtenbergs, Op. 37a, begun in 1996 and expanded for soprano and double bass in 1999. The cycle arose from his encounter with the private notebooks of Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, the 18th-century physicist whose intellect moved between experiment and satire. Never intended for publication, these “waste books” gathered observations whose brevity sharpened their reach. Lichtenberg’s scrutiny ranges across provincialism and religion, colonialism and literary history. Each joke becomes a trapdoor opening onto centuries of vanity. Kurtág began setting the aphorisms while ill, initially for solo soprano. Singer Maria Husmann encouraged the addition of double bass after experimenting with improvised accompaniment, a genesis audible in the finished cycle. Voice and instrument discover one another without settling into fixed roles. The bass accompanies before interrupting, then places a dark question mark beneath Lichtenberg’s wit. Fitz Gibbon and Miletich inhabited these relations with theatrical aptitude. The opening “Die Kartoffeln” (“The Potatoes”) was oddly beautiful in its evocation of slumbering tubers and their potential afterlife. “Kirchtürme” (“Church Spires”) rose through lovely pizzicato, its aspiration destabilized by the plucking that produced it. “Koan” became a fervent prayer edging toward cognitive seizure. Kurtág exposed the nervous system inside each of these, revealing the involuntary twitch beneath polished intelligence. That method reached sardonic clarity in “…und eine neue Welt…” (“…and a New World…”), where Fitz Gibbon sang through her teeth: “The American who discovered Columbus made a nasty discovery.” The reversal compresses colonial history into a grammatical ambush, exposing discovery as a story power tells about intrusion. Here, as elsewhere in the cycle, language appeared to turn against the assumptions concealed within its own syntax. Beecher’s stop-motion films, still a work in progress and therefore accompanying only selected aphorisms, extended this instability into a visual register. His reappearance as animator also gave the program a satisfying circular architecture. Having entered through his own music in With Grandchildren, he returned within Kurtág’s, translating acts of listening into movement and matter. Objects advanced through minute discontinuities, their apparent motion created by absences between frames. The art form therefore proved uncannily suited to Kurtág, whose music repeatedly asks the listener to construct continuity across charged gaps. Both forms make disappearance part of their syntax. The most persuasive union of image and sound came in “Ein Liebhaber der klassischen Philologie” (“A Classical Philology Aficionado”), concerning a man so enamored of Homer that he reads the German angenommen as “Agamemnon.” Books towered behind drifting clouds while statues looked on as thought acquiring mineral flesh. Beecher let the visual analog unfold slowly, giving the words time to expose the strange pathology hidden inside cultivated learning. Erudition became a benign haunting, a possession so complete that antiquity rewrote the present from within. The sequence clarified what the animations contributed to the cycle as a whole: they gave Kurtág’s microscopic dramas another surface upon which to misremember and mutate. The closing “Ein merkwürdiger Gedanke” (“A Strange Thought”) brought Kurtág’s humor to its darkest edge. Miletich and Fitz Gibbon allowed laughter to reveal its ancient kinship with fear. By then, one work had entered another through hidden roots. Cage’s knocks survived inside Kirsten’s tapping, while Beecher’s elderly voices continued inside Lichtenberg’s posthumous sentences. And through it all, Joyce’s sleeping forest returned in the Vermont woods surrounding the hall. The program cohered through subterranean recurrence, with each composition sending material below the surface for another to absorb. Marlboro’s seclusion ultimately changed the concert. Isolation became an acoustic form of relation, concentrating distant minds into one chamber. Beneath our feet, roots continued their exchanges without witnesses, each message altered by the body carrying it. The afternoon suggested that memory follows the same obscure traffic. We imagine ourselves as its custodians, although the reverse may lie closer to the truth. Memory could be the larger organism, ancient and unfinished, using each of us as a temporary organ through which to migrate. For one hour in Ragle Hall, voices became gills in that organism. items._cn_summary: 乐评聚焦于马尔伯勒音乐节呈献的库尔塔格世界专场，以女高音与低音提琴的极简编制展开。库尔塔格的音乐以极端压缩著称，寥寥数音承载戏剧重量，停顿使时间内卷，微型曲式在时钟之外形成独立的质量法则。评论将这种隐秘的经济学与佛蒙特森林的同心圆年轮相类比，声音成为语言之下过程的听觉末端。演出还纳入贝彻为孙女所作的曲目，其素材源自对多伦多与佛蒙特老年人的访谈，低音泛音营造不安的摇曳感，女高音在记忆的微妙失败中搜寻，使回忆成为一种由遗忘与保留共同塑造的不稳定行为。文章以诗化散文笔法深入探讨声响、沉默与注意力比例的变形，但文本在末尾被截断，未能呈现完整的演出分析与终曲评述。

items.body: Zwickau’s Elektrisch Festival returns on 24 October 2026 with a line-up that makes a convincing argument for electronic music as a continuum rather than a museum of separate generations. At one end stands Portion Control, active since 1979 and fundamental to the development of British industrial electronics; around them are Hungarian EBM veterans Escalator, the much newer KRIEG-B, and the contemporary projects OSZYLAYTER and Cyborg Projekt X. The 19th Elektrisch Festival takes place at Club Seilerstraße, Seilerstraße 1B, 08056 Zwickau. Doors open at 19:00, with the programme beginning at 20:00. The final line-up announced by organiser emmobiz Records is Portion Control, Escalator, OSZYLAYTER, Cyborg Projekt X and KRIEG-B. A festival with a rather unusual history Elektrisch is not a newly invented festival carrying an impressive number. Its history reaches back well before the current revival. Contemporary reports document the 11th edition in 2007, the 12th in 2008, the 13th in 2009, and two editions, numbers 14 and 15, in 2010, then held at Zwickau’s BPM Club. Artists appearing during that period included names such as Absolute Body Control, Birmingham 6, Tyske Ludder and The Klinik. Then Elektrisch disappeared for fourteen years. emmobiz Records revived it in 2024 with the 16th Elektrisch Festival, now at Club Seilerstraße. That return was already sold out months in advance and brought together Calva Y Nada, Cat Rapes Dog, Digital Factor and Accessory. The 17th edition followed in October 2025 with Test Dept, NZ, In Strict Confidence, Supreme Court and To Avoid. In February 2026, the 18th Elektrisch expanded across two evenings, separating a synthpop-oriented first night from a harder EBM/electro programme on the second. That history makes the 2026 autumn line-up apt: Elektrisch has repeatedly connected artists from different phases of underground electronic music instead of reducing EBM to one historical period. Portion Control The obvious historical heavyweight is Portion Control. Formed in London in 1979, the group emerged from the early British industrial-electronic underground and became important for its use of synthesisers, drum machines and sampling long before those methods became standard practice. Their influence has subsequently been acknowledged in connection with artists including Skinny Puppy, Front Line Assembly, Nine Inch Nails, Orbital and Nitzer Ebb; they also toured with Depeche Mode in 1984. But calling Portion Control a heritage act would miss what remains interesting about them. They returned in the 2000s and have continued producing new work rather than maintaining the early catalogue. This August they released “1983-86 – Hit The Pulse to Purge…”, their first major Artoffact archival box, while their official site simultaneously continues to define the project rather succinctly as “uncompromising dark electronic audio.” Zwickau is currently one of only two forthcoming live appearances listed on their Bandcamp. Escalator Escalator brings another kind of history to the evening. The Hungarian project was founded in Budapest in 1988 by 2RT+TB and belongs to the late-’80s/early-’90s generation of European Electronic Body Music. Its musical roots lie in the harder intersection of EBM and industrial electronics, with early influences including Kraftwerk, Throbbing Gristle, Cabaret Voltaire, Clock DVA and Front 242. Escalator’s history has been anything but linear; long gaps between releases and activity have been part of the project, yet its work has remained closely associated with the physical, stripped-back mechanics of classic body music. Their presence next to Portion Control is more than an “old-school” pairing: the two acts come from different geographical and chronological points in the development of electronic body music. OSZYLAYTER The German OSZYLAYTER represents a much more recent strand of the line-up. Public biographical information on the project is relatively sparse, so it is better not to manufacture a grand history that isn’t there. What can be verified is a growing Bandcamp catalogue including “Hate This Day”, “Lover Boy”, “Free Girls” and “Dig It in the Dirt”, while current Elektrisch coverage places the project on the modern dark-electro/industrial side of the bill. In the context of Elektrisch, that relative newness is actually useful. This isn’t five bands demonstrating variations of exactly the same established EBM formula; OSZYLAYTER helps shift the evening toward newer club electronics and shows where some of those older physical principles have travelled. Cyborg Projekt X Cyborg Projekt X is similarly one of the less extensively documented names on the programme. The confirmed festival announcement places the project alongside OSZYLAYTER as part of the contemporary dark-electro and industrial side of the line-up, with an emphasis on forceful, club-oriented electronics. That makes Cyborg Projekt X something of the unknown variable of the evening, especially for listeners arriving primarily for the established EBM names. In a festival whose history has always mixed recognised acts with smaller projects, that is hardly out of character. KRIEG-B KRIEG-B is much newer as a project but comes with considerable history behind its members. The duo was formed in June 2023 by Dominique Lallement, known from Kriegbereit, Cobalt 60 and K-Bereit, and Benoît Buyse, associated with Dreadfool, Anamorphosis and Nihiliste. The project describes its music as a meeting point between industrial electronics, EBM and darkwave, drawing on several decades of electronic music rather than one specific period. Their debut album “War Drums’ Resonance” arrived in November 2024, with tracks including “S.C.S.N”, “Parabellum”, “Artificial Minds”, “Truth Lies” and “King of Emptiness”. In a sense, KRIEG-B makes a neat closing piece to the Elektrisch concept: a young project constructed by musicians carrying several earlier generations of European industrial electronics with them. More than the line-up The revived Elektrisch has also developed a strong physical-release component. The 18th edition was accompanied by exclusive 10-inch festival vinyl releases, while emmobiz has already announced a V.A. “19. Elektrisch Festival” 10-inch connected to this year’s event. The appeal of the 19th edition goes beyond Portion Control finally returning to Zwickau. The five acts represent very different positions within the same broad history: British industrial experimentation, Hungarian old-school EBM, contemporary German dark electronics, and a new Franco-Belgian project carrying the experience of earlier industrial formations into something current. That is probably the strongest reason to pay attention to Elektrisch. After a fourteen-year absence, the festival did not return simply to recreate the period in which it originally existed. Its current identity depends on putting that history into the same room with what came after it. 19. Elektrisch Festival: date, venue and line-up Elektrisch Festival 24 October 2026 Club Seilerstraße Seilerstraße 1B, 08056 Zwickau, Germany Line-up: Portion Control Escalator OSZYLAYTER Cyborg Projekt X KRIEG-B Doors: 19:00 Start: 20:00 Tickets are available through emmobiz Records.

items.body: There’s always a moment when an artist with a reputation for electronic music severity discovers the cheap thrill of a perfect pop song, and Chances finds Kontravoid standing over the evidence with a butcher’s knife in his hand, dripping blood-red from your severed expectations. Behind that mask, it’s difficult to tell whether Cameron Findlay looks pleased with himself, but the hook suggests he’s been planning this for some time. Findlay has spent years making electronic music built from locked doors, hard angles, and basslines with the social instincts of a nightclub bouncer. Chances, the latest preview from Sound of the Void, due October 2 through Artoffact Records, loosens that grip without turning soft. There’s a trace of Cabaret Voltaire’s “Why Kill Time” in its marriage of electronic unease and pop temptation, the sense that a tune can slip something deeply questionable past you simply by making your hips complicit. The bassline supplies the charm, the synthesizers raise suspicions, and by the time the hook takes hold, you’re already eating a stranger’s piece of candy in the back of a white van. The surprise is not that Kontravoid can write pop. The surprise is how naturally this thing fits this masked marvel. The song opens with clipped, almost cryptic lines pushed through a harsh vocal treatment, Findlay’s voice sounding less sung than transmitted from some badly damaged communications device. Around him, warped synthesizers bend and smear, but the track never loses its discipline. The bass is lush and melodic, the electro beat keeps the body moving, and the arrangement has enough open space to let the hooks land cleanly. Then the verse seems to come apart at the seams. His voice gives way to a wash of effects and a series of shouts, as if the song has briefly forgotten the difference between a chorus and an alert from the Emergency Broadcast System. This is pop music with the wiring exposed. It has the sleek economy of synthpop, but Findlay refuses to sand down the abrasion that makes Kontravoid recognizable. The sinister pads and forceful rhythms still carry the weight of coldwave and EBM, only now they are being used in service of something broader, catchier, and frankly more dangerous because it might get stuck in your head before you realize how severe it is. That expansion also makes sense for a project that has never been as one-dimensional as the mask suggests. From Undone through Too Deep and Faceless, Findlay has always buried melody inside the machinery; Chances simply drags it forward and lets the damn thing breathe. Listen to “Chances” below and pre-order Sound of the Void, due out October 2 via Artoffact Records, here. Sound of the Void will be available digitally, on CD, and on clear vinyl. Sound of the Void by Kontravoid Following Detachment in 2024, Findlay’s second full-length for Artoffact gives melody more room to move through the Kontravoid universe, and Chances makes a persuasive case for taking the chance of leaving your doors unlocked. There’s a blade concealed beneath the song’s immaculate pop tailoring, however, and anyone attempting to call the genre police will find the phone line has been cut. Kontravoid is currently on tour in North America, co-headlining with Australian electronic artist Buzz Kull. The run concludes October 24 at the SUBSTANCE festival in Los Angeles. The October 2 album release falls on the tour’s Kansas City stop. Spike Hellis and Normal Bias will join the bill in Spokane, Vancouver, Seattle, Portland, and Sacramento. Tickets and further information are available through Kontravoid’s official website. items.body: With every breath Thru muck and grime In every trek We write … Greg Bullock has spent enough time around darkwave to know that gloom by itself is cheap, and on 26EP he treats darkness less as decoration than as a blunt instrument for asking ugly questions. Bullock, co-founder of Cyborg Amok, wrote, produced, mixed, performed, and illustrated this four-song set himself at GABWorx Studio B, which gives the record the slightly dangerous feeling of a man locking himself in a room with synthesizers, a bass, an electric mandolin, and several subjects polite company usually keeps under the table. There is nobody here to tell him that mortality, ecological collapse, betrayal, and human endurance might be a bit much for one EP, which is probably why the record has teeth. In Other Words starts with endurance, though Bullock does not turn survival into a greeting-card slogan. Trenches, mud, climbing, breath, effort: the vocabulary suggests a life measured by what it costs to keep moving. The song carries a reflective sweep that places Bullock somewhere between Depeche Mode’s electronic gravity and Roger Waters staring at civilization with his arms folded. There is comfort in the chorus, but the comfort has dirt under its fingernails. Then comes Thirty Pieces, which drags betrayal, punishment, commerce, and crucifixion into the same dry stretch of ground. Bullock uses biblical imagery with the instincts of someone less interested in Sunday-school reverence than in the ugly exchange rate between flesh and money. Silver gets thrown, bodies get displayed, peace gets its monument, and the entire arrangement starts feeling like one of those public ceremonies where everybody solemnly agrees not to mention who paid for the nails. I Ain’t Goin! is the EP’s great crooked grin. Bullock considers death and responds with the cosmic equivalent of hiding behind the couch when the landlord knocks. Angels can drag him away, Saint Peter can check his watch, and eternity can leave another message. Mortality remains right there in the room. Bullock’s electric mandolin and bass give the track a wiry, physical character, and its humour keeps the record from sinking beneath the weight of its own concerns. Blu-Green Beauty turns toward ecological collapse and corporate arithmetic, with burning seas, damaged forests, fossil fuels, solar panels, recycling, and the familiar human talent for closing the curtains while somebody else totals the profits. Bullock’s anger is clearest here, yet he keeps the song anchored to concrete images rather than vague righteousness. The result has the clipped moral unease of classic synth-pop filtered through the suspicious eye of someone reading the financial pages beside an environmental report. Across twenty minutes or so, 26EP keeps returning to responsibility: what we owe the dead, the living, the planet, and ourselves while there is still time to argue about it. Bullock’s hooks keep the philosophy from turning into homework, while his arrangements give each track its own shape and temperature. He has made a compact record about enormous subjects, and the best compliment is that none of them feel safely settled. Listen to 26EP below and order the EP here. items._cn_summary: Greg Bullock以Cyborg Amok联合创始人的身份推出个人EP《26EP》，四首曲目由他独立完成词曲、演奏、混音及封面创作。评论指出他深谙黑暗氛围之道，却拒绝将其作为廉价装饰，而是用沉重主题——死亡、生态崩溃、背叛与人类韧性——作为发问的钝器。开篇曲以Depeche Mode式的电子重力与Roger Waters式的文明审视融合，在坚韧与疲惫之间寻找平衡。第二曲引入圣经意象解构权力交易，第三首以电曼陀林和贝斯带来黑色幽默，第四首转向环境议题的道德不安。整体在二十余分钟内反复叩问责任：生者、死者、星球与自我之间的亏欠。评论内容较为完整，原文虽被截断但信息量充分，覆盖了每首曲目的主题与音乐特征。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: A confession to begin: I�ve been a fan of Alison Cotton�s music for quite a while, so the announcement of a new album definitely brought me a frisson of delight. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The centerpiece, however, is �Sprigs of Heather,� with an opening that recalls medieval sacred music that becomes a simple, slowly cascading, piano-led melody. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. It will challenge you but also satisfy and move you. What more can you wish from music? Find the artist online. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa厂牌推出的贝宁乐队Orchestre Poly-Rythmo与作曲家Antoine Dougbé的合作合集，收录1977至1982年间作品。Dougbé以拍击大腿演奏Cavacha节奏著称，其音乐融合伏都教仪式元素、刚果伦巴与古巴son的影响。评论指出，由于录音年代跨越七十年代末至八十年代初，音色呈现明显变化——吉他带有塑料质感，合成器开始进入编曲，但整体仍扎根于七十年代 funk 传统。文中以《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》为例，分析了合成器铺垫、闪亮吉他与踩镫主导节奏的层次交织；《We Tayi Sin Assi Tche》则展现了更直接的古巴风情，使用持续的牛铃与鼻音演唱的呼应结构。合集聚焦Dougbé短暂但浓烈的录音生涯，展现贝宁流行音乐与西非及拉美节奏传统的交汇。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. items._cn_summary: 这支乐队最核心的特点是用废弃物和零碎材料自制乐器——tassofons、tilofon、kitchenofon 等名字本身就是一种宣言。专辑将这些自造乐器投入多元风格的演绎中：克莱兹默小品里单簧管笑声般地领奏，非洲节拍段落散布着木鱼和摇铃，桑巴与昆比亚段落里长笛勾勒旋律，中东风格段落则带有六十年代谍战主题曲的恍惚气质。更值得注意的是，这些"垃圾乐器"在高精度录音下音准和音色都经得起考验，乐手在即兴段落中展现出扎实功底。整张作品在嬉戏与严肃之间找到平衡，既是文化融合的庆典，也是对音乐本质的反思——声音材料从不是障碍。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio的新专辑延续了前作《Eventyrferd》的探索精神，将传统挪威西部民间音乐与爵士即兴、现代电子声响相融合。主奏乐器高音萨克斯贯穿全作，叠加模块合成器与颤音琴的色彩层。乐队打破固定角色分配的传统模式，乐手之间频繁互换旋律主导与节奏支撑的位置，使得即便是源自springleik舞曲的素材也呈现出自由的即兴走向。低音提琴与鼓的节奏框架为即兴段落提供张力，而合成器的空间感则拓展了挪威民间旋律的当代维度。这张作品体现了斯堪的纳维亚音乐家在世界音乐素材与实验爵士之间寻找平衡的独特路径，既扎根于本土传统又具备开放的声音探索意识。

items._cn_summary: 普里斯姆四重奏发起的"释放你的内在作曲家"系列新作，由作曲家大卫·祖宾斯基创作，邀请诗人歌手厄休拉·拉克、打击乐手泰肖恩·索雷以及小提琴家卡洛斯·圣地亚哥共同参与编排与演绎。作品时长不到四分钟，从粗粝的原始质感出发，穿越抒情的旋律空间，最终回归初始状态，展现出精妙的控制力与充沛的能量。四位不同背景的音乐家在费城免费图书馆的现场演出中将古典室内乐框架、即兴爵士、人声吟诵与弦乐表达融为一体，是该系列跨界合作理念的一次集中体现。

items.body: Kr�ta , the latest release on Norway's Taragot label, features a Swede and two Norwegians playing interpretations of mainly traditional tunes from their respective countries. Fiddler Mats Ed�n has long been involved in Swedish folk music, as a player, composer and teacher, and in the process exploring and integrating different musical styles and approaches. Tellef Kvifte was in the pioneering Norwegian crossover band Slinkombas in the 1970s and has continued to play a central role in Norwegian folk music, both as a musician and an academic. Most often heard playing the sj�fl�yte , more widely known as a recorder, Kvifte has employed other instruments from outside the Norwegian tradition, in particular the saxophone and bagpipes. His son Knut Kvifte Nesheim , a drummer and composer, has also shown a determination to blur the lines between different musical genres, both in his solo and group projects. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio It comes as no surprise then to find this trio offering a far from conventional take on the tunes they have chosen. While dance tunes may be the source of most of the material here, this feels more akin to chamber music; not that it is remotely classical in style, but in the sense it conveys of three players engrossed in a musically intimate conversation. This is not a performance appropriate for accompanying dancers but might instead be seen as an exploration of hidden possibilities of meaning in the music. In so doing it reveals some of its underlying mystery, including, perhaps, a darker side. Just as in an Ibsen play, where the surface bonhomie, jollity and social nicety can be hiding something more sinister, in Scandinavian dance music there are at times hints of a troublesome undercurrent below the surface. So the decision to open proceedings with �Fossgrimen,� a fiddle tune from Norway's Setesdal valley, is perhaps significant. A fossgrimen is a mythical creature, a kind of water-sprite living in waterfalls from whom fiddle-players were considered to have learned their skills and for that were not universally welcomed, with the fiddle considered to be the devil's instrument. Kr�ta by Ed�n/Kvifte/Nesheim trio Tellef Kvifte takes the lead melody on most tracks but on the Swedish �Polska from Per Myhr,� having played a repeated introductory riff on the sj�fl�yte, with Mats Ed�n providing an amorphous textural accompaniment below and Nesheim adding some quiet tinkling, it's Ed�n who introduces the tune on the fiddle with Kvifte proceeding to play in unison. It's a short track and almost as soon as it gets going things start to fragment and everything grind to a halt.

items._cn_summary: 这是挪威Taragot厂牌发行的专辑，由一位瑞典小提琴家与挪威父子乐手组成的三重奏演绎两国传统曲调。评论指出作品虽源自民间舞曲素材，却摆脱了舞蹈伴奏功能，呈现出室内乐般的亲密对话感——三位乐手各自带有跨越流派的背景，包括民谣、爵士、教学与学术领域，因此对素材的处理远超常规演绎。专辑探讨了民间音乐表层欢快背后潜在的不安与阴暗面，以挪威神话中的瀑布精灵形象为隐喻。录音中可见器乐之间的层次织体：横笛与萨克管、铃鼓声部交织，小提琴在抽象伴奏中引入旋律后又迅速瓦解，展现出对传统素材的解构性重新诠释。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Andrew D'Angelo首张个人作品，整张唱片从头到尾仅使用低音单簧管一件乐器演奏。他在乐队合奏语境中以多乐器演奏者身份闻名，此作将低音单簧管推向绝对主角位置，完全释放这一乐器的表现潜力。文章将其称为'世界上最伟大的木管乐器'，强调低音单簧管在音色、动态、呼吸感等方面的独特魔法。低音乐器在爵士与即兴音乐中本就具备稀有的低频叙事能力，而单簧管家族又以复杂的泛音结构闻名。整张作品将这两重特质叠加，构成一张纯粹以低音单簧管为媒介的独白式即兴文本。

items.body: In his latest exploration of boundary-pushing traditional music from around the world, Patrick Clarke reports from Sweden’s Supertraditional Festival, where bridges are being built across Europe’s experimental folk scenes. Plus, 10 crucial new records, from Spanish electroclash bagpipes to Millinerian weirdness from Leeds Sara Parkman performs live at the inaugural Supertraditional Festival. Photo by Isak Gudnason Before we begin, I can't recommend enough that any England-based readers catch La Tène and Sourdure, two outliers of the French radical folk scene, at their forthcoming Cafe OTO show this Saturday (26 September). I reviewed La Tène live in my last column, and I stand by every effusive word, no matter how hyperbolic they might seem. It’s Pippi Longstocking day at Skansen, and several artificially-freckled... The post Radical Traditional: Folk Music for Autumn, by Patrick Clarke appeared first on The Quietus.
