items.body: Adrian Utley, the guitarist and co-founder of Portishead, has reworked “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” from Polish composer Mariusz Szypura’s “Chopin Residue,” a project that removes the piano entirely from nine of Frédéric Chopin’s best-known piano pieces. The rework arrives today as the latest single from the double album, which Cleopatra Records brings to CD and double vinyl on 16 October; an immersive Blu-ray edition mixed in Dolby Atmos is already available. Chopin Residue by Mariusz Szypura Szypura said working with Utley was a long-held ambition: “Adrian and Portishead are among my favourite musicians. The sound, the approach to making music, the search for unobvious and lo-fi textures, all of it had an enormous influence on me.” Szypura kept the harmonic structure and phrasing of Chopin’s originals while stripping out the instrument itself. He described the decision as a matter of respect rather than provocation: “I rejected the piano immediately. […] I decided Chopin didn’t deserve such profanation. I could only approach this material through the prism of my own sensitivity, harmony, and deconstruction. So I took the piano out. […] The piano was the delivery system, not the content.” Adrian Utley’s rework of ‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ “Chopin Residue” splits into two discs: “Deconstructions,” on which Szypura rebuilds nine Chopin pieces with a cast including Lee Ranaldo (Sonic Youth), David Pajo (Slint), Joey Waronker, Gail Ann Dorsey, John McEntire (Tortoise) and John Stanier (Battles), and “Reworks,” on which a second group of artists takes those deconstructed recordings further from the source. Utley’s “Étude Op. 25 No. 12” opens the second disc alongside reworks by Fennesz, Matthew Herbert, Masayoshi Fujita, Sean O’Hagan, Jim O’Rourke, Christine Ott, Benoît Pioulard and Abul Mogard. Szypura described the difference between the two discs directly: “‘Étude Op. 25 No. 12’ is Adrian’s reconstruction, not my piece with his guitar on top. That is the principle of the whole second disc: nine artists, nine rebuilds, each in their own language.” The two discs are designed to be played together as well as separately, an idea that extends into the Blu-ray edition’s Dolby Atmos mix. Szypura said: “They were built to overlap. […] In stereo you hear an arrangement. In Atmos you’re inside the harmonic space with the piano missing from the middle of it. […] That’s not a format upgrade, it’s closer to what the piece was always trying to do.” “Chopin Residue” gets its UK stage premiere at London’s Cadogan Hall on 26 September, as part of the Polish Jazz Festival. Its packaging has also picked up a Bronze A’ Design Award and a Red Dot Award. About Adrian Utley and Mariusz Szypura Adrian Utley was born in Northampton in 1957 and moved to Bristol in the mid-1980s, where he played guitar in touring bands led by jazz organist Big John Patton and drummer Art Blakey’s Jazz Messengers. He co-founded Portishead in Bristol in 1991 with Geoff Barrow and Beth Gibbons, co-producing and playing on the band’s albums “Dummy” (1994), “Portishead” (1997) and “Third” (2008). Outside the band, Utley has recorded and toured with Marianne Faithfull, Jeff Beck and Will Gregory of Goldfrapp, leads his own ensemble Adrian Utley’s Guitar Orchestra, and has scored film and audio work with director Nic Roeg, naturalist David Attenborough and Britain’s National Trust. Mariusz Szypura is a composer, producer and visual artist born in 1972 and based in Warsaw. He started out in the early 1990s in the Poznań rock band Happy Pills before founding his main recording project, Silver Rocket, releasing five albums including “Infinity Fidelity,” a Dolby Atmos record that won Gold for Music/Film Cover at the 2025 European Design Awards. His installation work includes “in:human” at the Centre for Contemporary Art Ujazdowski Castle in Warsaw (2024) and “êkhos” at Lincoln Center during Unsound Festival New York (2024). “Chopin Residue” grew out of that installation practice: Szypura first released the album digitally and on 2LP, 2CD, 2MC and Blu-ray through his own Black Element Label in Warsaw on 28 November 2025, alongside gallery and listening events in New York, Osaka, Los Angeles and Warsaw. Cleopatra Records now extends that release internationally, bringing “Chopin Residue” to CD and double vinyl on 16 October 2026 while the Blu-ray Immersive Edition remains available from its earlier release.

items._cn_summary: 波兰作曲家Mariusz Szypura的《Chopin Residue》项目对肖邦九首钢琴练习曲进行了去钢琴化的解构处理，仅保留和声结构与乐句走向，将原曲中的钢琴完全移除，以吉他、合成器、人声及其他乐器重建作品内核。专辑分为两张碟：'Deconstructions'由Szpura本人与Lee Ranaldo、David Pajo、John McEntire、John Stanier等独立及实验音乐人合作完成；'Reworks'则邀请Adrian Utley、Fennesz、Jim O'Rourke、Matthew Herbert等九位艺术家各自进行再度重构。其中Portishead吉他手Adrian Utley对'Étude Op. 25 No. 12'的重建被Szpura强调为独立创作而非简单叠加。专辑同时发行Dolby Atmos沉浸式蓝光版本，将'钢琴缺失的中空感'作为空间设计的核心概念。

items.body: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain. For Washington, D.C.’s Faeryn Johnson, the musician behind Faded Pulse, that uneasy invitation opens onto Elysia, a second album where ethereal wave, goth, folk, and dream pop meet the romantic imagination of medieval poetry and Victorian painting. Acoustic guitars, hammered dulcimer, electric bass, and ambient synthesizers accompany water spirits, waiting maidens, and woodland gatherings whose hosts have questionable intentions. The route here runs through the synthpop of 2025’s Submission and the more ethereal leanings of that year’s Fallen EP, with a decisive turn taken while watching Monica Richards perform with Strange Boutique in Washington. Johnson’s affection for the 1990s Projekt catalogue supplies another set of coordinates: Lycia, Love Spirals Downwards, Black Tape for a Blue Girl, and Unto Ashes sit alongside the folk of Pentangle and Donovan. There is a generous curiosity at work, the kind that can find room for both a Slowdive bassline and a William Morris poem without making either feel like an unlikely guest. Johnson’s background in art history gives Elysia a visual life as rich as its musical references. Waterhouse’s paintings, the Arts and Crafts movement, and Art Nouveau belong to the same imaginative world as thrifted velvet, medieval dress, and an old copy of Tennyson found in an antique shop. Beneath the finery lie practical questions about courage, community, and how to remain attentive to the living world. This gathering of fairies may be perilous, but the hope is that listeners return from it with a renewed appetite for their own lives. We spoke with Johnson about the records that opened those doors, the literature and paintings behind Elysia, and the enduring possibilities of ethereal music, from a hammered dulcimer to a dream performance among the art and architecture of the Cloisters. Before Faded Pulse, what first opened the door to the Gothic imagination for you? Was there a particular record, book, painting, or encounter that made you feel you had found somewhere you belonged? Faded Pulse: I started getting into the gothic scene when I was around 14 years old, and at that time my most essential record was The Cure’s Pornography. I loved the dense, almost psychedelic sound of the album. I’ve probably overplayed that record way too much at that age. Yet it really cemented my love for atmosphere and dense sound design. Robert Smith’s honest and vulnerable lyricism made me feel so seen and got me through so much. Between Submission, Fallen, and Elysia, your music has moved further into folk and ethereal wave. What was happening in your life and listening habits that encouraged that change, and what could you express through these arrangements that you hadn’t explored before? Faded Pulse: When I first started “Submission” around 2022, I was very much into the New Wave and Synthpop sounds of the 80s, and that really shows on that album, although my listening has always been more eclectic. One big influence on Elysia was psych and folk of the 60s and 70s, particularly bands like Pentangle; their album Solomon’s Seal was super influential on me, especially songs like “Willy O’Winsbury”. Donovan was another big influence; you can really hear it on songs like “Will Thy Heart Be True,” where I go for a more folky, ballad-type song. I have always had a huge love for the 90’s ethereal scene. The moment I knew I wanted to move sonically towards that was when I saw Strange Boutique live at the Black Cat in D.C. in 2025. Seeing Monica Richards on stage and hearing the music live was really a light-bulb moment for me. Ethereal allows me to experiment more with unusual instrumentation and also lets the music take people to another world. Although I enjoyed making synth pop, here I can play with classical, folk, ambient, and even more rock-oriented structures. It’s so much more playful and freeing. I feel like Faded Pulse would have been a perfect fit for Projekt Festival, especially the 1997 edition. How were you first introduced to the label and its artists, and was there a particular band or record that sparked your affinity for that strain of ethereal music? Faded Pulse: Projekt has a special place in my heart and is probably one of my favorite labels ever. My essential four artists from the record label are Black Tape, Lycia, Love Spirals, and Unto Ashes. Black Tape for a Blue Girl’s “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” is one of my all-time favs; it is a masterpiece in its own right in sound design and atmosphere, and it’s both deeply haunting and romantic. I feel like Love Spirals Downwards Idylls is glaringly obvious as one of the influences on Elysia, and I feel it is their most essential record. It’s hard for me to choose a Lycia album because they’re my favorite band on the label, but if I had to choose, it would be “A Day in the Stark Corner”. It’s equal parts dreamy, cold, and bleak. Unto Ashes serves everything I look for in a band: medieval instruments and sounds, folk and darkwave synths. I feel like their album “Empty into white” is so sonically rich and put together, sinister yet dreamy. I’m not sure how I even stumbled on the label, which feels fitting, like it came to me almost in a dream; it is the most influential group of artists for me. There’s something about Elysia that feels entirely at home in the pages of Propaganda or Carpe Noctem. What feels special to you about the Gothic culture of the ’90s, and how have you encountered that period through its music, magazines, photography, and fashion? Faded Pulse: Funnily enough, I own an issue of Propaganda, No. 22, and I wanna say it’s from 1994-1996. I have very fond memories of reading Propaganda magazines in high school on the Internet Archive. I am a historian at heart and love to learn everything I can about culture, music, and fashions of any time period I study. The 90’s, to me, feel somehow criminally underrated, even though it was when the gothic scene was at its peak and fully found itself and diversified into many different interests. I feel the worship of the 80s has caused people to overlook how creative the scene was in the 90s. Even now, somehow darkwave from the 90s is still more experimental and fresh than the very 80s-oriented sounds we get today. As for the fashion, I would study a lot of the pictures on Pinterest from magazines, club shoots, or people’s personal uploads, and when I went thrifting, I would look for similar items. PVC, Satins, Silks, and Velvet are all mainstays in my closet thanks to the 90s, haha. “Meadow of My Mind” and “Upon the Heavens” feel like a bridge between Cocteau Twins and the more romantic corners of the Projekt catalogue. How do you approach the relationship between voice and guitar in these songs, especially when both seem capable of carrying the melody or dissolving into one another? Faded Pulse: Much like the bands before me, I kind of treat the voice as just another instrument. When recording a lot of these songs, I wanted the guitar and voice to mesh well. In meadow of my mind, the voice and guitar switch throughout the song, giving them space to drive the song along without clashing. In “Meadow of My Mind,” you sing, “Leave this dying world behind,” yet you’ve described Elysia as something beyond escapism. What does that inner refuge make possible for you, and what do you hope listeners bring back from it into their everyday lives? Faded Pulse: To me, “Meadow of my Mind” is about the love of nature, to put it plainly. When listeners “Leave the realm of Elysia,” I want people to bring that sort of magic into their everyday lives. Whether that be getting involved in their local communities, making art, or reading poetry. Whatever it is that makes you feel connected to the world around you. “Upon the Heavens” uses the language of prayer, reaching toward a divine presence and asking to be heard and healed. What is your relationship with that devotional language, and how did you arrive at the kind of sacred experience you wanted the song to convey? Faded Pulse: To me, music is very spiritual, and I definitely wanted Upon the Heavens to emulate that in some way. It’s not a song devoted to a particular deity or religion, but it is about reaching out and feeling something greater. I feel this all the time through music, when I listen to a song that just makes me float away or feel high on euphoria. I mean, historically speaking, music is how people connect to the otherworld and is used in ritual, even though it is now far removed from its sacred roots. Music still feels deeply spiritual and otherworldly, and I think that’s truly what the song conveys. “Lamia’s Kiss” brings to mind Dead Can Dance’s exploration of musical traditions beyond rock, with an experimental quality that feels ancient and unfamiliar at once. Which specific traditions, recordings, or instruments informed it, and how did you develop its musical character? Faded Pulse: The sounds of the Middle East and the Mediterranean very much inspire Lamia’s kiss. A lot of the bands I liked, like Lovespirals, DCD, and Rajna, had eastern influence in their music, so it kinda bled into my consciousness. Rather than writing cliched lyrics about her as a figure, I wanted the song to emulate what it would feel like to be caught in her hypnotic gaze, to be pulled in. Instrumentally, I wanted the Dulcimer to be the lead on the song, which I feel really harnesses that archaic, almost ancient vibe that I wanted the song to have. I also grew up in Asia for a short time. I do think it had a musical effect on me, and it seems only natural that an experience like that would creep into my music in some way. What first drew you to Lamia as a figure? Did you come to her through mythology, Keats’s poem, a painting, or another interpretation, and what interests you about the meeting of beauty, desire, and danger in her story? Faded Pulse: It’s a little bit of all of that. Keats’s poem is definitely an inspo, as is Waterhouse’s iconic painting. I am also a Lilith and Hecate Devotee; the lamia is associated with both, so it’s almost devotional. I also love serpentine imagery and symbolism, as well as the figure of the femme fatale, so it is essentially a collage of many different ideas and feelings. “Fair Lady in Gold” has a baroque richness and a medieval atmosphere, particularly in the bright, struck-string sound that suggests a hammered dulcimer. How did you build that arrangement, and who—or what—is the lady at its center? Faded Pulse: For “Fair Lady in Gold,” I knew I wanted to have a few instrumental tracks on the album. The main instruments here are my Dusty Strings hammered dulcimer and my Korg Minilogue for ambient synths. There is no single song as an influence; rather, months and weeks of studying and listening to music from the Renaissance and medieval period that shaped this song. When I first started writing “The Lady in Gold,” I was envisioning Cordelia from King Lear in a painting by Edwin Austin Abbey. Although her gown is yellow, it is not even close to gold, haha. However, a woman with a golden pooling Bliaut gown was what I was envisioning when creating the song, so the name kinda stuck. “Summerland” seems to occupy a meeting place between Dead Can Dance and Cocteau Twins, while its lyrics describe being drawn into a fairy gathering. How welcoming did you want that invitation to feel, and how much uncertainty or danger belongs within its beauty? Faded Pulse: Summerland is definitely a song where I wanted the listener to be taken away by the fae, where it’s both exhilarating and panic-inducing. To be led away and dancing with beings who look human, yet there is something quite off about them, and strange things happen around them. I wanted to evoke the same feelings I had reading Irish fairy tales, where the stories of the fae are both wondrous and terrifying in equal measure. I think it’s a great metaphor for nature itself. Beautiful yet dangerous. “Undine” recalls the dreamier side of 4AD, alongside Faith and the Muse and Lycia, but its bassline and guitar flourishes also make ethereal wave’s goth and post-punk origins audible. How conscious are you of that connection when writing, and what does the bass allow you to do beneath such expansive arrangements? Faded Pulse: The bassline for Undine was heavily inspired by the bassline in Slowdive’s “Ballad of Sister Sue.” I knew I wanted this waltzy song where the bass carried much of the song’s sway. To me, the bass here is the most important; it just wouldn’t sound the same with a synth bass. It really gives the song that romantic rhythm I feel it needed. The words to “Undine” address the water-born figure directly, questioning her lover’s constancy and encouraging her to voice her feelings. Whose voice did you imagine addressing her, and what did you want your interpretation to reveal about her beyond the familiar tragedy? Faded Pulse: With Undine, I knew I really wanted to do a melancholic song about a siren, where the song itself is almost like a lament, where it feels like a spell is being cast onto the listener. The voice that carries the song is part third-person narrator and part Undine’s voice. The Chorus is nonsensical and is a made-up language, but it is Undine casting her spell, hoping and praying to keep Huldbrand’s love. The third-person voice beckons Undine to own her sadness and heartbreak to sing what’s in her heart and drown in her tears, tragically ending the knight’s life, but also having the strength to embrace her own emotions of love and betrayal. “Will Thy Heart Be True?” has the feel of an ethereal folk ballad, with its knight, waiting maiden, and tests of courage. Which Arthurian or medieval texts informed the song, and what does the question of remaining true mean to you personally? Faded Pulse: I think the concept of knight and maiden came to me through William Morris’s poem “Two Red Roses Across the Moon.” Although I’ve been a fan of Morris for a few years, I first heard of it when I visited the American Arts and Crafts Museum and saw a mural depicting the maiden from the poem waiting for her knight, who was off at war. Although I love the stereotypical depiction of the medieval romance trope, the song really isn’t solely about that. It is about staying strong during dark times and finding the courage to go on, which I feel is extremely relevant. Now, the question “Will Thy Heart be True?” is really asking, “Do you have the strength to keep fighting the good fight?” even when it seems hopeless. Your influences include Romantic literature, medieval poetry, and Victorian fairy tales. Which writers have most shaped your imagination—Keats, Christina Rossetti, William Morris, or perhaps someone less immediately expected? Could you take us through one passage or story that found its way into Elysia? Faded Pulse: One of my biggest influences was Alfred Lord Tennyson’s Idylls of the King, a book I thrifted in an antique shop. It features a poetic retelling of Arthurian legends, and although none of its stories made it into Elysia, I knew I wanted Elysia to evoke the feeling of magic, mystery, and romance that the book gave me. Poems like Coleridge’s Christabel and Keats’s La Belle Dame sans Merci were hugely influential as well. Keats’s story of the Faery woman leading the gullible knight astray was definitely an inspo for Summerland. Your art-history background brings the Pre-Raphaelites, Art Nouveau, and the Arts and Crafts movement into the album’s conception. Is there a particular work by an artist such as Burne-Jones, Waterhouse, or Mucha that you could place beside one of these songs and explain the connection? Faded Pulse: Rather than a single painting, artwork, or artist, Elysia sounds like the movements as a whole and what they were trying to achieve. To me, I want people to look at any art from any of those movements and instantly think of a song from Elysia. But if I had to choose an image to associate with the album, I would choose Waterhouse’s Ophelia, as it was one of the few paintings that made me think, “I want to make music that emulates how this painting feels.” Your photographs feature flowing robes, a circlet, a sword, woodland, and Gothic architecture. Which historical garments, designers, films, or figures inform your sense of dress, and how much of that appearance comes from making or adapting things yourself? Faded Pulse: A lot of Elysia’s costumes are based on a combination of different things. For me, it was studying fashion history throughout the Middle Ages, a lot of the Medieval revival clothing coming out of the goth scene in the 90s, and of course, fantasy films like The Lord of the Rings (Particularly the elves). Photographs of Lisa Hammer and Monica Richards in the 90s and 00s were also influential on me. To me, Lisa is a modern Pre-Raphaelite fashion icon, and I definitely wanted to emulate that for Elysia. A lot of the wardrobe for the photos was thrifted or modified to achieve that vibe. What do you think made ethereal wave such a natural home for medieval romance, folklore, and mystery? Within your own music, what do those older forms of imagination allow you to say about love, longing, or belonging in the present? Faded Pulse: I think there’s something very classic about medieval folklore and stories. They feel very timeless with their usage of romance, bravery, and fighting for something you think is worth fighting for. They capture what it means to be human and to be alive. I think Medieval and Ethereal are so drawn to each other because they both have a sense of whimsy and otherworldliness. I think this element of fantasy is so unique to Ethereal outside of the other core genres of the gothic scene. With ethereal, I can weave stories and ambiance that fully immerse the listener into the world I want to create, and I think that’s why fairytales and ethereal go so well together; it’s a perfect mesh of storytelling and sonic immersion. An enduring part of the Gothic imagination is its embrace of mystery and the wonders of nature. Do you feel that connection is more important than ever in this age of AI, and what role can music play in keeping that sense of wonder alive? Faded Pulse: I think music is more important now than ever in the age of AI. It requires you to engage no matter what, to let go, sit down, and spend your time listening, to feel something. I think music is intrinsically human, and I feel that when people go out to clubs or venues for shows and connect with those around them, it really helps them disconnect from the haze of being online all the time and brings them into the present. There is something magical about watching people perform and bring something out of you. That is something that AI could never replace. If you could present Elysia in a setting entirely of your choosing, what would a Faded Pulse performance look and feel like? How would the space, clothing, and instrumentation help bring listeners into these songs, and what would you want them to feel when they stepped outside again? Faded Pulse: I think two of my dream performance locations would be a medieval ruin or within the Met Cloisters Museum in New York. I feel like being surrounded by actual medieval art and architecture would really set the ambiance. One thing I’ve heard of is that bands in the 90s would have incense burning on stage. I don’t know how true that is, and of course, venues would never allow that now, but I think something like frankincense or sandalwood would be my chosen scent, and I feel like playing with multiple senses would really elevate the performance. For dress, I think it would be cool to have a lot of the new-agey medieval revival looks from the nineties that were popular in the scene, and, of course, I would encourage everyone to participate in dressing up if they so choose. For me, I want the audience to feel like they entered another realm, dreamy and untethered, and when they leave, feeling like they had a spiritual awakening.§ For all its mythic tales of knights, faeries, and enchanted waters, Elysia is an album that keeps returning to the ordinary work of being present: listening closely, making something, finding courage, and spending time with other people. Johnson’s ideal audience might gather in velvet beneath medieval arches, but the invitation extends well beyond that imagined evening. There is room for wonder in a borrowed book, a local show, or an afternoon among the trees, and Faded Pulse offers plenty of reasons to make room for it. Faded Pulse’s Elysia is out now. Listen to the album below and order here. items.body: EXAUDI Pocket Universe Four pieces by Cassandra Miller, Andrew Hamilton, Leo Chadburn and Geoff Hannan under the baton of conductor James Weeks Curation is everywhere nowadays: from art biennales to food menus, everything has abespoke theme, bolstered by snazzy presentation, marketing ploys and influencer campaigns. But what happens when you release music without a thematic lynchpin holding things together? Such is the case of Pocket Universe, the most recent offering from the vocal ensemble EXAUDI and conductor James Weeks, released on NMC Recordings. It comprises four pieces by Cassandra Miller, Andrew Hamilton, Leo Chadburn and Geoff Hannan, commissioned by EXAUDI’s annual EXPOSURE showcase between 2013 and 2019. items.body: Ms Xxan released the nine-track album “Make Yourself the Lie” on September 8, 2026, via VuMantra Records, available as a free, name-your-price download on Bandcamp. Ms Xxan performs the album’s spoken word poetry herself, processing her voice through synthesized effects and building the backing from dark ambient and noise-industrial soundscapes, with every credit on the record, from writing through final mix, going to her alone. The album carries a content warning for strong and explicit lyrics; depression under present-day conditions runs through its themes, and the nine tracks grow steadily heavier as the sequence progresses: “make yourself the lie.”, “psychic break.”, “doctrine of harm.”, “dissociative parallels.”, “crossing over.”, “discontinuance.”, “disremember.”, “anhedonia.” and “hatchling.” The same material is also published in episode form as the “Ms Xxan” podcast, available on Apple Podcasts and Audiomack, and streams on SoundCloud alongside the Bandcamp release. Make Yourself the Lie by Ms Xxan About Ms Xxan Ms Xxan writes and produces spoken word and industrial noise music from her current base in the Pacific Northwest, a home she plans to leave before long. “Make Yourself the Lie”, released September 8, 2026, is her album for VuMantra Records, a Berlin-based label founded by Vū (Vince Gagliardi) in 2019, who also records as The Nent and LAGÁN. VuMantra describes its output as “endarkening rhythms for dystopic sub-cultures”, with a catalog built on percussive, ritualistic and tribalistic electronic music. “Make Yourself the Lie” was written, performed, composed, produced and mixed entirely by Ms Xxan, and stands as her first release documented on the label alongside the parallel “Ms Xxan” podcast series carrying the same material.

items.body: German medieval techno act Klangschmiede & Friends released the single “Remember” on September 1, 2026, and submitted it as an application for Germany’s national selection process for the Eurovision Song Contest 2027. The full application was uploaded to public broadcaster SWR on the same day; German participation in the 2027 contest is not yet confirmed. Live bagpipes, hurdy-gurdy and flute sit alongside electronic production on “Remember,” with English lyrics and passages in Old High German drawn from early medieval sources such as the Hildebrandslied. The track runs just under three minutes and moves between medieval techno, dark electronic production and historical folk balladry. Klangschmiede & Friends’ Eurovision 2027 bid For the submission, Klangschmiede expanded into the extended line-up Klangschmiede & Friends, bringing in additional musicians for the song’s acoustic instrumentation. The official music video was filmed with the full ensemble at Schloss Burg in Solingen on August 17, 2026. Regional public broadcaster WDR was on site for the shoot and aired a television feature on the production through its Lokalzeit Bergisches Land program. The submission has also drawn coverage from ESC kompakt and regional newspapers including the Solinger Tageblatt and the Remscheider General-Anzeiger. About Klangschmiede Klangschmiede is the duo of Claudia Sokoll and Timo Tofaute, based in the Bergisches Land region of Germany and operating officially since 2025. The project mixes medieval and Nordic folk elements with electronic production, drawing on historical sources such as the Hildebrandslied, the Poetic Edda and Nordic ballads. Its catalog includes the album “RITUS”, released digitally and on CD on May 14, 2026, and singles including “Nothing We Love Is Ever Gone” (March 26, 2026), “Hüter der Straße” (April 30, 2026) and “Solringen” (July 23, 2026), alongside a remix of “Tanz den Feuertanz” featuring Keltania. Klangschmiede has also worked with the medieval folk-rock band Corvus Corax on the track “Ragnarök”. “Remember”, released as a single on September 1, 2026 under the expanded name Klangschmiede & Friends, is the project’s submission for Germany’s national Eurovision Song Contest 2027 selection, with participation still to be confirmed.

items._cn_summary: 德国双人组Klangschmiede（Claudia Sokoll与Timo Tofaute）将中世纪与北欧民间音乐素材与电子制作结合，2026年发布专辑《RITUS》及多支单曲。其欧视参赛作品《Remember》以扩展阵容Klangschmiede & Friends呈现，引入风笛、手摇风琴与长笛等原声乐器，配合电子制作，歌词使用英语并援引古高地德语段落，取材于《希尔德布兰特之歌》等早期中世纪文本。音乐在暗黑电子、中世纪Techno与历史民谣叙事之间游走，时长不到三分钟。音乐视频于索林根城堡取景，由WDR地方节目报道。项目曾与中世纪民谣摇滚乐队Corvus Corax合作《Ragnarök》，并与Keltania合作混音作品，显示出对中世纪音乐素材系统性的探索与跨风格合作倾向。

items.body: Italian musician Ystrith released the seven-track dark ambient debut album “The M Rites” on 2 September 2026, self-issued on Bandcamp and also available on Spotify. Across its seven tracks, Ystrith works with Mithraic mystery-cult imagery, the Roman-era worship of the god Mithras, pulling on details like its buried temples and the weathered carvings its followers left behind. The M Rites by Ystrith Ystrith described the album to Side-Line as concerned not only with the surviving relics of the Mithraic cult, but with “the unbridgeable distance between the surviving objects of the cult and the experiences that have been lost with time.” The seven tracks – “Cautes”, “Fading Gates (of Cosmic Enlightenment)”, “Marble Tauroctonies”, “Myth of the Petrogenesis”, “Voces Magicae”, “Solstice at the Spelaeum” and “Cautopates” – take their titles directly from Mithraic iconography and ritual: Cautes and Cautopates are the torch-bearing twin attendants of Mithras in Roman relief carvings, while “tauroctonies” refers to the bull-slaying scene at the centre of Mithraic imagery. Ystrith has described the record’s musical language as moving through “slow metamorphoses, obsessive repetition and dark, suspended atmospheres,” sustained across the album’s running time to match its ritual subject matter. About Ystrith Ystrith is an Italian musician who records ambient and dark ambient music. “The M Rites”, released 2 September 2026, is the project’s debut album, presented as a sustained meditation on the Mithraic mysteries rather than a single-themed track or EP. The release is available to stream on Bandcamp and Spotify.
items._cn_summary: 意大利音乐人Ystrith的首张专辑以古罗马密特拉教为题材，构建了七轨的黑暗氛围冥想。七首曲目分别撷取密特拉崇拜的核心意象——双火炬手Cautes与Cautopates、屠牛图景Tauroctonies、冬至石窟Solstice——将仪式符号转化为声音作品。音乐语言围绕缓慢的形态演变、偏执的重复循环与悬浮的黑暗氛围展开，与密特拉教仪式中神秘、封闭的精神体验相呼应。自述关注的不仅是教派遗留的实物残片，更是这些遗存与已经失落体验之间无法跨越的距离，将考古学的沉思注入声音设计之中。整体呈现出一种概念驱动的仪式氛围创作。

items.body: Manufracture Music release the single “System Apathy” on 20 October 2026, under a pre-order campaign already live on Bandcamp. The Vienna-based project, run by producer Valerian Steel, built the track entirely on analog synthesizers, drum machines and raw voltage, with no software instruments involved. System Apathy by Manufracture Music The Bandcamp description describes the release as continuing the project’s A.C.I. concept, short for Analog Core Industrial: “Manufracture Music operates on a strict hardware-first philosophy. […] Forged in Vienna, ‘System Apathy’ is built entirely on unforgiving analog synthesizers, drum machines, and raw voltage. The physical behavior of the machines – their limitations, imperfections, and textures – becomes the composition itself.” Steel described the approach directly to Side-Line as “a cold, relentless EBM transmission born from technological friction and dystopian sound design.” Manufracture Music’s second A.C.I. release “System Apathy” follows “The Scene Lies (A.C.I. Manifesto)“, the two-track statement Manufracture Music released on 14 August 2026 that introduced A.C.I. as a stated concept: hardware-only production positioned against generative AI tools in the electronic underground. Where that release took the form of a spoken-word manifesto, “System Apathy” returns the project to song form while keeping the same zero-software constraint. About Manufracture Music Manufracture Music is the industrial, EBM and darkwave project of producer Valerian Steel, based in Vienna, Austria. He also runs the dance-oriented Fourtyfication*5 and the ambient-leaning Music of Synergia under his own name, and has worked with a vocalist credited only as Enzo across several Manufracture Music tracks. The debut album “Fractured Empires” appeared in early 2025, followed by the “Mormon” EP on 29 March 2025 and a run of singles through 2025 and 2026, including “Isolated”, “Ghosts” featuring Enzo, “Blood Syntax”, “Hateration”, “Tearfall”, “End of Life”, “Null Rite System” featuring Enzo, “Kinetic Decay”, “Skip My Tracks” and “Synthetic Species”. “The Scene Lies (A.C.I. Manifesto)” introduced the A.C.I. concept on 14 August 2026, and “System Apathy” now becomes the second release built under that same hardware-only method, due 20 October 2026.
items._cn_summary: 维也纳制作人Valerian Steel的Manufracture Music项目以A.C.I.（模拟核心工业）概念为基础，发布单曲《System Apathy》。整首作品完全使用模拟合成器、鼓机和原始电压信号构建，不涉及任何软件乐器，强调硬件设备的物理局限、瑕疵与质感本身成为作曲素材。从概念宣言《The Scene Lies》到这首回归歌曲形式的单曲，硬件优先的方法论被一以贯之地执行。作为A.C.I.框架下的第二作，作品延续了对生成式AI工具的明确反对立场，以冰冷的工业律动与末世感声音设计为核心表达。该项目同时涵盖EBM、暗潮、工业、氛围等不同侧面的子计划，体现了制作人在电子音乐谱系内的多线探索。

items.body: Pray for me tonight Blinded by your light Stigmatize my mind Your lost paradise Anton, a Parisian post-punk project led by Anton Steinbock, carries itself with the severe romanticism of someone who owns more black coats than practical shoes, but their recent single Répression finds that severity loosening into something stranger, more fevered, and considerably more dangerous. Working with fellow coldwave artist Tout Debord, Steinbock pushes his music toward a place where devotion and psychic collapse keep borrowing each other’s clothes, while Leonid Diaghilev’s production gives the track enough space to breathe without sanding away its cold edge. The guitars ring out in pale, eerie streaks, recalling Clan of Xymox during their 4AD era, while the bass keeps the floor beneath everything firm and deliberate. Synths reminiscent of Asylum Party and Little Nemo deepen the song’s French coldwave character, and its brooding melancholy brings to mind Scottish band Lowlife. Anton keeps these affinities personal through Steinbock’s low, echoing delivery and the movement between French and English. His voice sounds less like a performance than a private argument accidentally amplified through the walls of an empty Church. This tension suits the lyrics, which circle despair, fixation, religious need, and the exhausting effort of trying to escape thoughts that have already memorized the route home. Emptiness becomes almost physical here, while religious language turns love into a strange transaction involving devotion, punishment, salvation, and sacrifice. There is a plea buried inside the song, though Anton wisely lets it remain uneasy. Comfort carries a price, paradise looks compromised, and the promise of another night together begins to resemble a trap with excellent lighting. Tout Debord’s video takes those concerns and gives them a suitably Catholic mindspace. Performance footage is layered over religious images, cemeteries, stone, and monuments, with additional cinematography by Sylvester Engbrox adding another layer of distance between the body and whatever eternity is supposed to mean. The images of permanence become almost sarcastic beside a song obsessed with emotional states that keep mutating by the hour. Faith may promise forever; the people on screen still have to get through tonight. Watch the video for Répression below: Répression also marks a useful turn after Never Freed Myself, continuing Anton’s taste for austere post-punk while sharpening the drama and widening the frame. Since the project began in 2024, Steinbock has moved quickly from solo recordings to a live configuration with Gabriela Guyez, building a set that can pivot from harder post-punk material toward synth-heavy darkwave ballads. Répression works best as a collision between movement and paralysis: the body gets the beat, the mind gets the bad news, and the track keeps one boot planted firmly on the dance floor. Anton has made a song for anyone who has ever mistaken obsession for revelation and then had to live through the morning after. Listen to Répression below and order the single here. Répression by Anton, Tout Debord Follow Anton: Bandcamp Spotify Facebook Instagram YouTube The post “Pray For Me Tonight” — Anton and Tout Debord Share Video for French Coldwave Confessional “Répression” appeared first on Post-Punk.com.
items._cn_summary: 巴黎后朋克项目Anton与同侪Tout Debord合作的单曲以冷波美学为底色，将宗教意象与心理崩溃交织成一段近乎告解的文本。制作人Leonid Diaghilev为器乐留出呼吸空间，吉他音色苍白冷冽，合成器层叠出法国冷波特有的忧郁质感，贝斯则稳固地托住整体结构。Steinbock低沉回声式的人声在法语与英语之间游移，歌词围绕执念、救赎与情感寄生展开，将亲密关系描述为一场涉及虔诚、惩罚与牺牲的诡异交易。MV以教堂墓地等宗教视觉叠加表演画面，形成与歌曲情绪呼应的张力。歌曲延续了Anton此前作品中的苦行式后朋克倾向，同时扩展了戏剧化表达，在身体律动与精神麻痹之间制造碰撞。整体而言，这是一篇文笔生动、参考系丰富的乐评，精准定位了作品在冷波谱系中的坐标，但音乐本身更接近类型化呈现而非突破性实验。

items.body: Purest Form Resistance Dais Records Despite its brief fifteen minute runtime, there’s a meal to be made out of LA trio Purest Form’s latest EP, their debut on Dais, both in terms of attitude and presentation, as well as what its selection of very clear influences might portend for the larger post-industrial landscape. Drawing upon familiar markers of 90s electronic aggression, Resistance provides a tight test case for their read on that historical moment. Opener “Animal” functions as a strong calling card for Purest Form, showing both their capacity for a catchy, heavily processed guitar riff as well as Story Beeson’s acidic growl that’s part grindcore, part death metal. Factor in just the right amount of backing programming and an easily chantable chorus and it becomes both cathartic and anthemic in short order. It is, to be glib, exactly the type of thrashing industrial rock glory which KMFDM have been failing to recapture for the past couple of decades. Much of the rest of the EP’s made up of densely programmed two-minute wipeouts jammed up with breaks, more heavily processed guitar now functioning more for colour than riffs, and more spleen and vile being vented. If that sounds on paper fairly akin to digital hardcore, listening to “Break” and “More” will do little to dissuade that presumption. “Beyond Terror” acts as a quick riposte to this frenetic pace, offering post-hardcore chug while the vocals cut through equivocations about the killings of Palestinians – “call it what you like, it’s genocide.” And then there’s the closing cover. Fifteen or twenty years back, an industrial metal act doing a straightforward version of The Prodigy’s “Breathe” would have felt awkwardly retrograde. However, a full three decades on from the original release and overdriven into the red to the point that it’s difficult to distinguish original tracks from sampled ones, Purest Form’s take on “Breathe” feels like the best sort of “oh shit, they’re covering this?” moment at the end of a packed and sweaty basement show. In discussing the appeal of the 90s sources Pures Form borrow from it’s important to not overstate how new they might be to the band; both Beeson and guitarist/programmer Madi Woodward both have lengthy rap sheets with slews of hardcore and metal acts going back a decade or so. But there’s no question that a combination of their backgrounds beyond industrial and the historical space separating Resistance from those acts helps invigorate their dense and furious angle on them. Buy it. RESISTANCE by PUREST FORM The post Purest Form, “Resistance” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._cn_summary: 洛杉矶三人组 Purest Form 在 Dais Records 旗下发行的首张 EP 仅十五分钟，却密度极高。开篇曲将处理过载的吉他 riff 与 grindcore/death metal 式的咆哮嗓音交织，配合程式化鼓击与合唱式副歌，形成宣泄式的工业硬核范式。后续曲目以两分钟左右的密集编程为骨架，吉他更多作为音色装饰而非旋律主导，整体偏向数字硬核的速度感与侵略性。中段插曲放慢节奏，引入后硬核式的切分节奏，歌词直指巴勒斯坦议题。终曲以过载处理翻唱 The Prodigy 的经典，在失真与采样边界模糊的状态下完成致敬。乐评指出乐队成员此前活跃于硬核与金属场景，其工业取向更多是当下历史语境与个人背景的交汇产物。

items.body:
There is a substantial list of attributes that sets Ran Blake apart from every other innovative pianist of the past sixty-plus years, each of which falls under one of two headings: his choice of materials and his treatments of them. The former is based on Blake’s ability to hear connections between materials for which “disparate” is an inadequate descriptor. Who else would sequence Max Roach’s “Mendacity” and “Saving All My Love for You” – or “On Top of Old Smokey” and Michel Legrand’s “Watch What Happens”? Nobody, because what Blake does is unique. He doesn’t interpret materials as much as administer an MRI, revealing the connective tissues and vital organs as vividly, if not more so, than the skeletal structure. In the process, Blake makes the familiar sound radically new.

Blake’s collaborations with singers are central to his work. The current critical consensus is that his groundbreaking work with Jeanne Lee overshadows everything since, the respective qualities of notables like Christine Correa and Sara Serpa notwithstanding. Roots & Byways circumvents the edifice The Newest Sound Around has become, primarily because Dominique Eade takes a different tact. She is not as rooted as Correa – or Lee, for that matter – in Billie Holiday, and she is not as committed to understatement as Serpa. Like both Correa and Serpa, Eade can shape a song syllable by syllable and render a highly personal interpretation. It is Eade’s palpably deep joy in singing that sets her apart, one that is not only bursting at the seams on showstoppers like the Whitney Houston megahit, but one that even seeps into noirish songs like Mingus’ “Portrait.” It is the key to her relatability and appeal, and to that of the album, as well.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以钢琴与声乐的二重奏为核心，展现了Ran Blake独特的选曲眼光和演绎逻辑。他将马克斯·罗奇、米歇尔·勒格兰等风格迥异的作品并置，用类似医学扫描的方式剥离熟悉旋律的骨架，暴露出不同音乐之间的隐秘关联。Dominique Eade作为合作歌手，延续了Blake与Jeanne Lee开创的钢琴-人声模式，但走出了一条个人路线：她的演绎比Christine Correa更具古典根基，却比Sara Serpa更为外向饱满，歌唱中流露出的深层喜悦赋予唱片极强的感染力。专辑在showstopper类型的曲调中展现充沛爆发力，同时也能在Mingus等色彩阴郁的作品里渗透出微妙的温度。整张唱片呈现出一种学院派爵士对曲库进行结构性重组的思路，既非标准爵士经典翻奏，也非纯粹的自由即兴，而是介于精心编排和直觉诠释之间的第三条道路。

items.body: Sudan Dudan is a Norwegian duo, Marit Karlberg and Anders Erik R�ine, who have released four albums over the last twenty years. On M�rke refrenger , their fifth, they are joined by Hans Hulb�kmo and Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard, contributing instrumentally and with the production. There are eight songs on the album with accompaniment principally led by acoustic guitar, augmented by fiddles, langeleik, lyre, jaws harp and more. The opening track, �Gard og grind� (�Fence and gate�) is a fine introduction to what is to come: finger-picked acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and snare-drum played with brushes leading into the harmonized vocal, together creating an alluring sound drawing the listener in. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The mood of the album, reflected in its title which translates as �Dark Refrains,� is not always dark, but most of the material, including the title track, certainly has a reflective quality. According to the press release �the lyrics smoulder with unease about the present and the future, while looking back to the myths and riddles of the past. They speak of the earth, the sun, the moon, stars and planets, of lost brothers, quarrelling sisters, loss and grief, of the power of imagination, and of the answers to the simplest and most difficult riddles.� The lyrics of all the songs, in Norwegian, are included in the sleeve notes and while a hasty online translation can aid with some understanding, the full meanings tend to remain cryptic, but there is a sense that words and music complement each other. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan For all its dark moodiness, M�rke refrenger does have its lighter moments. �Bagatelle� recalls and reinvents the melody of a well-known French song, adding some off-kilter harmonies, while �Rulleball� is more characteristically Norwegian, employing a vocal style known as tralling in which words are replaced by a vocalization of the melody, originally used to accompany dances when no instrument was available. No translation necessary there. M�rke refrenger by Sudan Dudan The final track �Skriften p� veggen� (�the writing on the wall�) features, for the only time on the album, electric guitar. The sound is deep and twangy, shades of Duane Eddy or a David Lynch soundtrack and it works very well. All in all a fine, imaginatively conceived and beautifully produced record, available as a download or vinyl. Find the artists online. items._cn_summary: 挪威二人组合Sudan Dudan的第五张专辑《Mørke refrenger》（黑暗副歌），由Hans Hulbækmo和Magnus Skavhaug Nergaard参与乐器演奏和制作。专辑共八首歌曲，以原声吉他为主，辅以小提琴、挪威传统乐器langeleik、里拉琴、口弦等。歌曲全部使用挪威语演唱，歌词围绕大地、太阳、月亮、星辰、失落、悲伤、想象力等主题展开，充满对当下与未来的不安，同时回望古老的神话与谜语。评论指出专辑整体氛围沉静内省，但并非全然阴暗，部分曲目呈现出较为轻盈的特质——如《Bagatelle》借用法国民歌旋律并加入不和协和声；《Rulleball》运用挪威传统的tralling人声技巧，以无词的旋律哼唱替代歌词。终曲《Skriften på veggen》是唯一使用电吉他的曲目，深沉而带有twang感的音色令人联想到Duane Eddy或David Lynch的配乐。整体制作精良，融合挪威民谣传统与现代编排手法，是一张富有想象力与文化深度的作品。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑聚焦于俄罗斯占领区约两万乌克兰儿童被强制带离父母的真实事件，以传统与原创歌曲交织的方式呈现这一战争罪行。乌克兰-加拿大歌手Marichka联合两支音乐团体录制，加拿大全女子组合Daughters of Donbas负责巡演。音乐上以弓弦乐器为核心，辅以班杜拉琴、钢琴以及从被毁城市马里乌波尔归来的被绑架少女Lisa演奏的双陶笛，器乐编排简洁而克制。曲目《Foreign Land》改编自传统民歌，歌词讲述母亲送女儿去陌生土地做工的历史叙事，与当下被拐儿童形成双重隐喻，Marichka的演唱温柔内敛。另一首《Rusalka》由Alina Kuzma主唱，风格转向强烈粗粝，引用乌克兰民间传说中的自然精灵鲁斯alka形象，传统仪式歌曲旋律被赋予尖锐的现代表达。整体而言，专辑将口述历史、民歌传统与当代政治语境融合，是一份兼具音乐性与社会关怀的声乐文献。

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items.body:
Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

items.body: Review by Rysiek P. — An opportunity like this certainly cannot be overlooked. Twenty years after releasing their debut album, *Armed Forces of Simantipak*, the band Khatsaturjan?whose name derives from the renowned Armenian composer Aram Khachaturian?has released a new record titled *Monolog Chronosa*. Their discography also includes two other albums - *Disconcerto Grosso* (2010) and *Beast, Machine & Man* (2015) - and their history is notable for the fact that, as early as their 2002 debut single *Aramsome Sums*, they performed their own "rock" versions of Modest Mussorgsky's *Night on Bald Mountain* and Hector Berlioz's *March to the Scaffold*. All of this was presented in progressive hard-rock arrangements that incorporated elements reminiscent of the band Gentle Giant. Furthermore, critics hailed the group's first album as a benchmark for symphonic rock. One might pessimistically remark, "But that was years ago". Yet, it is certainly worth checking out where Khatsaturjan stands today. The band's latest release comprises forty-seven minutes of music spread across seven tracks, with an album title suggesting that the passage of time is the central theme. This phenomenon is observed and described from various perspectives - including, perhaps most importantly, the human condition and the personal, often highly subjective experience of life passing by. The title of the opening track - "Lessons (On Human Obsolescence)" - gives one food for thought right from the start. However, do not expect dark, atmospheric arrangements here. The composition is remarkably balanced,almost conservative in its playing style and employs familiar progressive rock tropes, with one notable exception: a strong emphasis on vocal polyphony (a true hallmark of this album) and a more prominent role for keyboards. These two elements define the musical structure of the song, which opens with the sound of a bell before embarking on a progressive journey rich in engaging tempo shifts and instrumental virtuosity. The second track, "What Was True," takes a slightly different approach. Here, the band clearly leans toward a modern progressive sound, successfully utilizing "new textures" to craft a unique atmosphere that straddles the line between atmospheric progressive rock (or even neo-prog) and a vocal-harmony-driven ballad. Once again, vocal polyphony and synthesizers serve as the building blocks for both this specific track and the album as a whole. The track "The Dystopian Spirit Of Club Energy" also features a piano-and-synthesizer-driven sound. Yet, in this composition, the band draws upon classical music and classical time signatures. The piano sets the arrangement's course, serving as a backdrop for highly impressive vocal performances. Only halfway through does the track remind us that it is 2026, showing how a guitar-driven rhythmic boost can yield a truly successful result. Incorporating electronic elements into the arrangement only enhances the musical value of this piece, which runs over five minutes in length. It was only while listening to "Song Of Days" that I realized what truly draws me to the band's music: a delicacy and almost theatrical storytelling style, skillfully blended with classical influences, alongside magnificent tales sung with a masterful, gradual build-up of vocal intensity. With a full arsenal of musical tools at their disposal, Khatsaturjan selects only those that fit the symphonic-progressive narrative, all while keeping classical music traditions close at hand. "Song Of Days" is a perfect example of this approach. It makes brilliant use of symphonic arrangements, blending them with flawless vocal lines and weaving in thoroughly modern progressive guitar motifs to create a truly well-crafted track. "DID Memoir" shares a similar, song-oriented character. It opens with a "classic" sense of grandeur, progressive guitar work, and... such delicate vocals. Everything weaves together into a structure that challenges the listener - filled with improvisational passages that hark back to classical music and, as an added bonus, theatrical farce-style interludes appearing midway through the fourth minute. Just listen closely around the five-minute mark for a dose of rap; this element, yet another instance of the piece's stylistic multiplicity, is entirely justified given the title: "DID Memoir." While the acronym refers to Dissociative Identity Disorder, it also serves as a fitting title for the track's eclectic, multi-stylistic nature. Following a symphonic opening, the penultimate track on this magnificent album - "The Keepers of the Philosopher's Stone" - simply sends shivers down the spine with its superb vocal lines. It features backing vocals, humming passages, and a lead vocal that stands out tonally, its rough timbre lending an air of deep mystery. Yet, what makes this composition truly exceptional is the extensive and successful incorporation of motifs drawn from classical music; the violin sounds and classical time signatures transform this five-plus-minute piece into a remarkable puzzle of motifs and an intricate arrangement. A madrigal-like character, blended with thoroughly modern synthesizer and guitar sounds, seems to elevate the track's central theme - fittingly so for a song about the "Philosopher's Stone," which here truly transmutes individual notes into "gold." With this release, the end comes all too soon. Were it not for the fact that the closing track - "Mundus Meus (This World of Mine)" - employs every possible device to captivate the listener from the very first note, one might feel that the magnificent preceding track left something musically unresolved, a void that could neither be filled nor replaced. "Mundus Meus..." stands as a magnificent anthem and the perfect culmination of the album; the Latin lyrics sound both prophetic and majestic without detracting from the depth of the message. And although the track features numerous gentle prog-metal solos, it remains, at its core, a thoroughly symphonic-progressive composition. If I say that I am very - truly very - pleasantly surprised by the latest work from the group Khatsaturjan, is that recommendation enough? If not, I'll add that the band features essentially the same lineup as on their debut and subsequent albums, even though musical light-years have passed since that first release (in 2002). Atte Kurri (vocals, bass, keyboards), Ilkka Piispala (vocals, drums, keyboards, bass), and Ilkka Saarikivi (vocals, keyboards, bass, violin) continue to demonstrate that musical trends don't matter to them. It is significant that Khatsaturjan is a group of friends who get together only when they want to record something; they are not a band that makes a living from touring and recording albums. On their Facebook page, the band writes: "We work slowly because Khatsaturjan is not our profession - it is a passion project and a beloved hobby. Whenever we decide to work on a new album, we know a years-long effort lies ahead, with no financial reward whatsoever. Yet, time and again, we take on new projects." Perhaps this approach allows them to maintain a sense of detachment and find the tranquility needed to create new music? You surely know that things tend to flow more easily when there are no deadlines hanging over your head. And since we will likely have to wait a long time for the next sign of musical life from Khatsaturjan, we should simply enjoy this highly successful release - one that has earned a spot in my top ten albums of the year.

items._cn_summary: 亚美尼亚乐队Khatsaturjan时隔二十年发行新专辑《Monologue of Chronos》，以时间流逝为母题展开七首共四十七分钟的曲目。乐评指出作品风格偏向保守与平衡，并未追求黑暗或氛围化的极端走向，而是延续了其将古典名曲改编为前卫硬摇滚的传统。键盘与复调人声成为贯穿全专辑的核心支柱，取代了早期作品中更突出的吉他驱动结构。某些曲目向现代前卫与新前卫靠拢，融合电子元素与古典节拍；钢琴与合成器构建出层次丰富的声景，半程后加入的吉他节奏为乐曲注入当代感。整体而言，这是一张以人声复调与键盘为主导、兼具古典根基与现代前卫审美的专辑，适合喜爱Gentle Giant式精致编排的听众。

items.album: Sandie Trash announces ‘Poupée Panik’, featuring Eric Debris and Richard Belgium
items.excerpt: Sandie Trash announces the single “Poupée Panik,” featuring Eric Debris (Métal Urbain) and Richard Belgium (MI6), the first track revealed from the upcoming album “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka.” The French post-punk and new wave project has not confirmed a release date for the album itself, and “Poupée Panik” is not yet available on Sandie Trash’s Bandcamp page, Instagram or Facebook. Sandie Trash builds ‘Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka’
items.body: Sandie Trash announces the single “Poupée Panik,” featuring Eric Debris (Métal Urbain) and Richard Belgium (MI6), the first track revealed from the upcoming album “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka.” The French post-punk and new wave project has not confirmed a release date for the album itself, and “Poupée Panik” is not yet available on Sandie Trash’s Bandcamp page, Instagram or Facebook. Sandie Trash builds ‘Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka’ around the Motel Dakota The nine-track album is set around a recurring fictional location, Room 17 of the Motel Dakota, with several tracks written as character pieces tied to that setting: “La perversita,” “Poupée Panik,” “Élégance déplacée,” “Gloria Dakota” and “Sophie qui aime les avions.” Sandie Trash describes the record as a “sabotage” of eighties nostalgia rather than a nostalgic homage to the decade. Alongside Eric Debris and Richard Belgium, the album credits a wide cast of guest contributors: Emmanuelle 5 (Dead Sexy), Olivier de Joie (Les Fils de Joie), Max Freeth (Ausgang), Karbokroma, Kelsey Warren (Blak Emoji), Jérôme Lefdup (Lefdup & Lefdup), Gilles Le Guen (Denner) and Oli Le Baron (Ici Paris). One track, “I Trash You Fuck Off,” is credited with a guest vocal from Helno, the former Lucrate Milk member who went on to front Les Négresses Vertes until his death in January 1993. Sandie Trash’s announcement does not explain how that vocal appears on a track dated 2026, whether as a sample, an archival recording or another arrangement, and no further detail was available to confirm it. Eric Debris also mixed and mastered the album at ATX Mastering studio. The cover art is by Italian illustrator Volt.B. About Sandie Trash Sandie Trash is a French punk and electro project based in Périgueux, fronted by the singer of the same name and built, album after album, around a rotating cast of guest musicians on individual tracks. The approach dates back at least to 2018, when the project’s “Le French Peep Show” paired a new musician with each song on the record. On Bandcamp, Sandie Trash’s confirmed discography includes the album “Outrageous brune,” released 25 February 2010 through Indies.Music.Productions with vocals from Sandie Trash and Maudd and mixing and mastering by Emmanuel Borie, and the 14-track compilation “Rose chewing-gun & Machine-gum (2006-2017),” released 29 May 2025 and gathering tracks and features from that decade, including contributions from Kloot Per W, Romeo Praly, Kim Ohio Fuzz, Marcel Vanthilt and Nina Courson. “Poupée Panik” and the album built around it, “Jeunes filles mödernes & Bazooka,” continue that same collaborative format on a larger scale, bringing in musicians tied to Métal Urbain, MI6, Ausgang, Denner and other underground post-punk and EBM circles for a post-punk and new wave record set inside the fictional Motel Dakota.
items._cn_summary: 本文为法国后朋克与新浪潮项目 Sandie Trash 新单曲及专辑的发布消息，而非乐评。专辑以虚构地点 Motel Dakota 第17号房间为核心概念，多首曲目以该场景中的角色为创作出发点，被定位为对八十年代怀旧情绪的'破坏'而非致敬。合作阵容涵盖地下后朋克与 EBM 圈层，包括来自 Métal Urbain 的 Eric Debris、MI6 的 Richard Belgium、Denner 的 Gilles Le Guen、Ausgang 的 Max Freeth 等。专辑采用每首歌配一位客座乐手的合作模式，由 Eric Debris 在 ATX Mastering 工作室完成混音与母带处理，封面由意大利插画师 Volt.B 绘制。文中特别提到已故 Les Négresses Vertes 主唱 Helno 的客串声部出现在 2026 年的作品中，其使用方式未获说明。整体为独立地下厂牌发行，面向小众听众，但文章本身为新闻通讯，缺乏音乐分析维度。

items._cn_summary: 德国制作人Marcel Dettmann即将发行全长专辑《My Own Shadow: Album》，这是他时隔四年的首张完整作品，共收录19首曲目，横跨house、techno、electro、EBM与ambient等多种电子音乐脉络。专辑部分灵感来自他本人音乐之外的视觉创作，将声音与图像艺术进行跨界关联。前两张EP《Approaching》（2025）与《Faultline》（2026）已先行在!K7厂牌释出，为专辑铺陈。制作人在声明中表示，并不期望听众以特定方式理解这张专辑，而希望每个人能从中获得属于自己的感受，整体定位偏向开放式的感官体验而非叙事化表达。

items.body: Black Sherif takes his own sound apart on SUN SHERIF, the six-track EP he released through Blacko Management and EMPIRE in early September. The Konongo-born singer and rapper calls it “a deconstruction of everything Black Sherif’s done sonically“, a method that gives him the obsession he says he needs when working through fifteen or twenty demos at a time. That sound took shape on the “First Sermon” and “Second Sermon” singles of 2021, Twi verses set over highlife melody and UK drill drums, and in 2022 “Kwaku the Traveller” carried it to number one on Apple Music in Ghana and Nigeria. Two albums followed, The Villain I Never Was in 2022 and Iron Boy in April 2025. The EP brings in the Ghanaian singer AratheJay on “Forever” and the Trinidadian production duo Full Blown on “Love Again”, and Sherif sings “Jolie” alone, moving between Twi and English towards a chorus built on the French word for pretty. The verses are made of small acts of devotion: a New Year’s drive to her door, songs written for her in the manner of Kurt Cobain, a habit dropped because she disliked it. Listen to “Jolie” HERE and stream SUN SHERIF following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Black Sherif – Jolie appeared first on Rhythm Passport.
items._cn_summary: Black Sherif 来自加纳库农戈，以特威语说唱融合英国钻洞鼓点和高life旋律，2021年凭"First Sermon"和"Second Sermon"奠定声线风格，2022年"Kwaku the Traveller"在加纳和尼日利亚冲上Apple Music榜首。这张六曲EP是他对自己既有声音的解构，邀请加纳歌手AratheJay和特立尼达制作组合Full Blown合作。标题曲"Jolie"以特威语和英语交织，围绕法语"漂亮"之意展开，副歌在双语言间滑动。歌词记录日常爱意片段：新年驱车前往她门前、模仿库尔特·柯本为她写歌、因她不喜欢而戒掉某个习惯。整张EP强调自我声音拆解与重组的过程，旋律与鼓点的跨大洲拼贴是非洲新生代流行音乐中较为独特的处理方式。

items.excerpt: Review by Abrasmatheus — Wish You Were Here is one of those albums that does not need to be excessively complex to feel progressive.
